title: Rethinking Circuit Evaluation: Do Circuits Explain Model Errors?
question: Under mean ablation on GPT-2 small indirect object identification, did circuits agree with the full model's exact answers more or less often on prompts it got wrong than on prompts it got right?
methods: A manual circuit and several automated circuits for indirect object identification in GPT-2 small were evaluated with the rest of the model mean-ablated. Exact answer agreement between each circuit and the full model was measured separately on prompts the model answered correctly and on prompts where it erred.
option_a: Circuits agreed with the model more often on its errors than on its correct answers.
option_b: Circuits agreed with the model less often on its errors than on its correct answers.
evidence_quote: On indirect object identification (IOI) for GPT-2 small, under mean ablation, the manual circuit and tested automated circuits, including one trained against the model's full output distribution, agree with the model on 97.3-99.5% of prompts it answers correctly but only 11.4-41.7% of errors.
notes: Headline phenomenon: circuits miss the model's errors.

title: Emergent phases of superposition: from partial to full representation
question: In a toy model of superposition, did non-uniform feature firing probabilities raise or lower the loss compared with uniform firing probabilities?
methods: Anthropic's toy model of superposition was analysed with a partial random projection approximation and in experiments, varying model width, the number of active features and the distribution of feature firing probabilities. The loss and the critical width of the transition from partial to full feature representation were measured.
option_a: Non-uniform firing probabilities raised the loss.
option_b: Non-uniform firing probabilities lowered the loss.
evidence_quote: Non-uniform firing probabilities delay the transition and lower the loss, as more frequent features occupy more space.

title: Where Do LLMs Decide to Break the Rules? Mechanistic Localization of Prompt Injection Compliance
question: Was the rank of the linear subspace carrying prompt-injection compliance larger or smaller in a 32B model than in 4B and 14B models?
methods: Layer-by-layer causal activation patching was applied to five models from 4B to 32B parameters under prompt-injection attacks. The compliance mechanism at the causally decisive layer was approximated by a low-rank linear subspace, and the rank required was compared across model sizes.
option_a: The compliance subspace rank was larger at 32B than at 4B and 14B.
option_b: The compliance subspace rank was smaller at 32B than at 4B and 14B.
evidence_quote: We show that the compliance mechanism occupies a compact linear subspace (rank-8 in 4B and 14B models, scaling to rank-64 at 32B) and is architecturally stable across varying model families.

title: Decoding the Functional Roles of Register and High-Norm Patch Tokens in Vision Transformers
question: In DINOv2, did disrupting the top-activating SAE features derived from register tokens change the representation more or less than disrupting those derived from high-norm outlier patch tokens?
methods: Sparse autoencoders were trained separately on register-token activations and on high-norm outlier patch-token activations of DINOv2. The top-activating features of each were disrupted, and the resulting drop in representation cosine similarity was compared.
option_a: Disrupting register-derived features changed the representation more than disrupting outlier-derived features.
option_b: Disrupting register-derived features changed the representation less than disrupting outlier-derived features.
evidence_quote: Causal ablations fur- ther reveal a substantial functional asymmetry: disrupting top-activating register-derived features produces a 48.17% drop in representation cosine similarity, whereas disrupting outlier-derived fea- tures produces only a 0.31% drop.
notes: The abstract contains line-break hyphenation ('fur- ther', 'fea- tures'); the quote reproduces it verbatim.

title: ScopeSAE: Model-Scope Feature Discovery with Interpretable Layer Selection
question: When an SAE trained on gradient-selected token-layer states had its reconstructions written back into the model, was next-token cross-entropy lower or higher than with the original activations?
methods: Instead of one SAE per layer, an SAE was trained on one token-layer state per token, chosen by normalized gradient attribution scores. Its reconstructions were written back into the forward pass, and next-token cross-entropy was compared with that obtained from the original activations.
option_a: Cross-entropy with the written-back reconstructions was lower than with the original activations.
option_b: Cross-entropy with the written-back reconstructions was higher than with the original activations.
evidence_quote: Written-back reconstructions of the SAE produce lower next-token cross-entropy than the original activations, an outcome that, to our knowledge, has not previously been reported for SAEs.

title: Separators Make Carry Propagation Learnable:The Geometry of Latent Carry in a Multiplication Transformer
question: In small transformers trained on 4x4-digit multiplication, were the middle output digits learned earlier or later in training than the other digit positions?
methods: Small Llama-style transformers were trained from scratch on 4x4 multiplication without chain of thought, with a separator token between digits. The point in training at which each output digit position was learned was tracked, and the internal carry representation was studied with activation patching.
option_a: The middle digits were learned earlier than the other positions.
option_b: The middle digits were learned later than the other positions.
evidence_quote: Output positions are learned in carry-chain order, with the middle digits, which have the longest-range dependencies, learned last.

title: Do Vision-Language-Action Models Understand Instructions? A Mechanistic Interpretability Study on Language Grounding
question: In two vision-language-action models, were action outputs more or less sensitive to directional language in corrupted instructions than to abstract rephrasing?
methods: LIBERO task instructions given to pi-0.5 and GR00T N1.7 were corrupted in five ways: synonym replacement, semantic scaling, directional corruption, random object substitution and empty string. Activation and attribution patching on the residual stream of the action-generation modules measured how much each corruption affected the generated actions.
option_a: Actions were more sensitive to directional language than to abstract rephrasing.
option_b: Actions were less sensitive to directional language than to abstract rephrasing.
evidence_quote: Our experiments find that both models are comparatively insensitive to abstract rephrasing and to referencing non-existent objects, but react strongly to empty task descriptions and, especially, to directional language.

title: What Do Sparse Autoencoder Feature Discovery Scores Identify? From Activations to Interventions
question: For single-latent SAE ablations with nonzero effects, did gradient-based predictions match the realized sign of the effect more or less often than changes implied by linear probes?
methods: Across four model-SAE pairs, the first-order effect of ablating a single SAE latent on the model output was estimated with a gradient-based intervention attribution and, separately, implied from linear-probe coefficients. The sign of each prediction was compared with the realized effect of the ablation.
option_a: Gradient predictions matched the realized sign more often than probe-implied changes.
option_b: Gradient predictions matched the realized sign less often than probe-implied changes.
evidence_quote: For single-latent ablations with nonzero effects, gradient predictions match the realized sign in 91-97% of cases, compared with 17-35% for probe-implied changes.

title: Evaluating the Causal Faithfulness of SHAP as a Candidate Attribution Method for SAE Features
question: On minimal pairs with known ground truth, did attribution methods over SAE features detect inserted sentiment signal more or less reliably than they localized deleted sentiment signal?
methods: On SST-2 sentiment classification with GPT-2 Small and a 32,768-feature layer-7 SAE, SHAP, Integrated Gradients, Gradient x Input and probe-weight attributions were computed over SAE features. On minimal pairs in which a sentiment signal was inserted or deleted, the ability of the attributions to identify the changed signal was scored by AUROC.
option_a: Attribution detected inserted signal more reliably than it localized deleted signal.
option_b: Attribution detected inserted signal less reliably than it localized deleted signal.
evidence_quote: Second, under known-ground-truth minimal pairs, attribution recovers inserted sentiment signal well above chance (AUROC $0.792$) but fails to localize deletions (AUROC $0.520$), suggesting that these methods detect the presence of a feature's influence more reliably than its absence.

title: Readout Scaling Shapes Sparse Feature Recovery
question: On three language-model checkpoints, did SAEs trained on centered logits reconstruct output logits better or worse than SAEs trained in readout-canonicalized coordinates?
methods: SAEs were trained either on centered logits or in readout-canonicalized decision-space coordinates, a transformation defined from the singular values of the model's readout. On three fixed language-model checkpoints across 18 task-sparsity settings, the two kinds of SAE were compared on gain-free reconstruction and on reconstruction of output logits.
option_a: Centered-logit SAEs reconstructed output logits better than readout-canonicalized SAEs.
option_b: Centered-logit SAEs reconstructed output logits worse than readout-canonicalized SAEs.
evidence_quote: On three fixed language-model checkpoints, RC-DS has higher mean gain-free reconstruction in all 18 tested task-sparsity settings, while centered-logit SAEs reconstruct output logits better in 17.
notes: The readout-canonicalized coordinates (RC-DS) are the paper's own method; it wins on gain-free reconstruction but loses on logit reconstruction in 17 of 18 settings.

title: Sparse Transformer: a Controlled Testbed for Mechanistic Interpretability
question: In a sparse-MLP transformer whose neurons serve as a known reference basis, did transcoders recover the neuron vectors with higher or lower cosine similarity than sparse autoencoders?
methods: A 5-layer language model was trained on TinyStories with a wide TopK-sparse MLP so that its MLP neurons provide a reference basis. Transcoders (trained to map MLP input to MLP output) and sparse autoencoders (trained to reconstruct MLP outputs) were fitted to the model and compared on the cosine similarity between their learned features and the true neuron vectors.
option_a: Transcoders recovered the neuron vectors with higher cosine similarity than sparse autoencoders.
option_b: Transcoders recovered the neuron vectors with lower cosine similarity than sparse autoencoders.
evidence_quote: This testbed allows us to directly compare feature learning methods: Transcoder, which approximates the MLP input-output mapping, recovers ST's neuron vectors with 52.6% higher cosine similarity than Sparse Autoencoder, which only reconstructs outputs.

title: Causal Syntax Circuits in CodeLMs: Budget and Probe Decide What Looks Localised
question: Was code models' default preference for Python syntax, when the prompt names no language, larger or smaller in instruction-tuned checkpoints than in their base versions?
methods: Ten open code models (five base, five instruction-tuned) were prompted to write code without a specified language, and their preference for Python over a target language (Rust, C# or PHP) was measured with aligned prompts. Each instruction-tuned checkpoint was compared with its base version.
option_a: The Python preference was larger in instruction-tuned checkpoints than in their base versions.
option_b: The Python preference was smaller in instruction-tuned checkpoints than in their base versions.
evidence_quote: First, the preference is large, grows with model size, and survives instruction tuning: it is larger on every instruction-tuned checkpoint than on its base version, by 12% on average.

title: Entertain, then Cancel: How Thinking Makes Reasoning Models Read Some and Or Literally
question: When reasoning models were allowed to think longer, did they draw the pragmatic 'not all' inference from 'some' more or less often?
methods: With weights fixed, several open reasoning models and GPT-5 were run with different amounts of thinking before answering questions that test scalar and disjunctive implicatures (e.g. whether 'some' implies 'not all') as well as context-driven inferences. Their reasoning traces were also cut at successive points to elicit answers and locate where the reading changes.
option_a: With more thinking, models drew the 'not all' inference more often.
option_b: With more thinking, models drew the 'not all' inference less often.
evidence_quote: Thinking makes models read logical words as logic: it cancels the implicatures of \emph{some} (\emph{not all}) and \emph{or} (\emph{not both}) in most tested open reasoning models and in GPT-5, while context-driven inferences such as indirect answers improve.
notes: Mechanistic study of reasoning traces rather than activations; included under interpretability of reasoning models.

title: Do LMs Know What Variables Do? Interpreting Code Representations via Variable Roles
question: Across five model-SAE systems, did individual SAE features predict the roles of variables in code better or worse than linear probes on the residual stream?
methods: 11 variable roles from an independently defined taxonomy (e.g. accumulator, stepper, best-so-far holder) were annotated in 126,926 code files across five programming languages. Recovery of these role distinctions was compared between linear probes on residual-stream activations, individual SAE features and lexical baselines, across five model-SAE systems.
option_a: Individual SAE features predicted variable roles better than residual-stream probes.
option_b: Individual SAE features predicted variable roles worse than residual-stream probes.
evidence_quote: Across five model-SAE systems, residual probes outperform individual SAE features and tested lexical baselines, with modest losses after neutral target renaming.

title: Do LMs Know What Variables Do? Interpreting Code Representations via Variable Roles
question: Were probes trained on SAE reconstructions more or less sensitive to role-changing code edits than probes on the original activations?
methods: Linear probes for variable roles in code were trained on residual-stream activations and on the SAE reconstructions of those activations. Both were tested on source edits, reviewed by LLMs, that change a variable's role, and their sensitivity to these edits was compared.
option_a: Probes on SAE reconstructions were more sensitive to role-changing edits than probes on the original activations.
option_b: Probes on SAE reconstructions were less sensitive to role-changing edits than probes on the original activations.
evidence_quote: Combining SAE features closes much of the single-feature gap, but probes on SAE reconstructions are less sensitive to role-changing edits reviewed by LLMs.
notes: The comparison with probes on the original activations is implied by the abstract's contrast with residual probes.

title: Comparing Sparsified MLPs and Transcoders: Many Transcoder Features Are Neurons in Disguise
question: Across 13 open-source transcoders, did features not aligned with individual MLP neurons vary more or less between training runs than neuron-aligned features?
methods: Transcoder features whose weights strongly align with individual MLP neurons were labelled neuron features. Across 13 open-source transcoders, neuron and non-neuron features were compared on their consistency across training runs, their match to the MLP's Jacobian and their change from random initialization.
option_a: Non-neuron features varied more between training runs than neuron features.
option_b: Non-neuron features varied less between training runs than neuron features.
evidence_quote: Only neuron features have a stable correspondence with something in the underlying MLP: other features vary more between training runs, do not match the MLP's Jacobian, and change less significantly from their random initialization.
notes: Headline phenomenon: transcoder features that are stable are neurons in disguise.

title: How Language Models Organize Task Information
question: Did instruction-tuned deployment increase or decrease the number of features needed to recover most of a dense linear probe's performance?
methods: Readout sparsity was measured as the smallest number of features, found by a fixed search protocol, that recovers 95% of a dense linear probe's above-chance AUROC. It was computed for 19 language models from five labs on 14 tasks, comparing base models with their instruction-tuned deployments.
option_a: Instruction-tuned deployment increased the number of features needed.
option_b: Instruction-tuned deployment decreased the number of features needed.
evidence_quote: Instruction-tuned deployment selectively reduces \(k^*\), with both weights and input format contributing.

title: Behavior Beyond Text: Evaluating Refusal Transfer Failure in LLM Agents
question: In tool-enabled contexts, did activations along a refusal-associated residual-stream direction rise or fall relative to plain chat contexts, in most of five models?
methods: Matched harmful and benign requests were presented to five models in a plain chat setting and in tool-enabled settings. A refusal-associated direction was identified in each model's residual stream, and activations along it were compared between the chat and tool-enabled versions of the same requests.
option_a: Activation along the refusal direction rose in tool-enabled contexts.
option_b: Activation along the refusal direction fell in tool-enabled contexts.
evidence_quote: We find that in tool-enabled contexts, the activations along this direction decrease in four of five models.

title: Building Auditable AI Text Detectors with Sparse Autoencoders
question: On out-of-distribution texts, did a lightweight classifier on auto-labelled SAE features of an AI-text detector perform better or worse than the original fine-tuned neural detector?
methods: SAEs were trained on the residual stream of a fine-tuned neural AI-generated-text detector; their features were auto-labelled, and kept if the descriptions passed a fidelity threshold. A lightweight classifier trained on the kept features was compared with the original neural detector and with stylometric classifiers on out-of-distribution texts.
option_a: The feature-based classifier performed better than the neural detector on out-of-distribution texts.
option_b: The feature-based classifier performed worse than the neural detector on out-of-distribution texts.
evidence_quote: Classifiers built on these extracted features are not only highly interpretable but exhibit stronger performance on out-of-distribution texts than either neural or stylometric alternatives.

title: Rethinking SAE Evaluation: An Atomic Interpretable Unit Framework Reveals Hidden Polysemanticity and Redundancy
question: Across hundreds of SAEs, were the features contributing most to model computation more or less interpretable than other features?
methods: Hundreds of SAEs across several architectures and model families were evaluated with existing interpretability metrics, and their features were ranked by their contribution to model computation. Interpretability and redundancy were compared between the top-ranked features and the rest.
option_a: The most dominant features were more interpretable than other features.
option_b: The most dominant features were less interpretable than other features.
evidence_quote: Evaluating hundreds of SAEs across multiple architectures and model families, we uncover failure modes in which some SAEs appear monosemantic under existing evaluation metrics while remaining functionally polysemantic: the most dominant features, those contributing most to model computation, are systematically less interpretable and more redundant.
notes: Headline phenomenon is hidden polysemanticity of dominant features.

title: REACT: Representational Early Analysis and Control of Chain-of-Thought Trajectories
question: On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, did a one-time safety-direction edit to a chain-of-thought hidden state have a larger or smaller effect when applied at the fourth and fifth tokens than within the first two to three tokens?
methods: Safety directions were learned from paired safe and unsafe reasoning trajectories, separately for each of the first five chain-of-thought positions, in three distilled reasoning models. Each direction was added once to the hidden state at its position with frozen weights, the rest of the output was regenerated without further edits, and the change in fully safe outputs was compared across positions.
option_a: The edit had a larger effect at the fourth and fifth tokens than within the first two to three tokens.
option_b: The edit had a smaller effect at the fourth and fifth tokens than within the first two to three tokens.
evidence_quote: Across three distilled reasoning models and three generation seeds, the strongest gains concentrate in a two- to three-token early window; on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, the effect falls to approximately zero at the fourth and fifth tokens, even though later states can be more predictive of risk.

title: Depth-Dependent Safety Geometry in Vision-Language Models: Layer-Wise Localization and Bidirectional Refusal Control
question: In Qwen3-VL-4B, was refusal more or less responsive to activation steering along a learned safety direction at deeper layers than at early vision layers?
methods: A safety direction was learned from activations of Qwen3-VL-4B on safe and unsafe inputs. Activation steering along this direction was applied at different depths, from early vision layers to deeper layers, and the change in rejection of unsafe inputs was measured, together with how well each layer separated safe from unsafe inputs.
option_a: Refusal was more responsive to steering at deeper layers than at early vision layers.
option_b: Refusal was less responsive to steering at deeper layers than at early vision layers.
evidence_quote: Deeper layers remain well separated along the safety direction yet are largely insensitive to steering, distinguishing representational separability from causal controllability.

title: What Survives Distillation? A Mechanistic Interpretability Study of GPT-2 and DistilGPT-2
question: After depth-reduction distillation from GPT-2 to six-layer DistilGPT-2, was more or less of the teacher's task performance retained on indirect object identification than on the greater-than task?
methods: GPT-2 and its distilled six-layer student DistilGPT-2 were compared on two well-characterised circuits, indirect object identification (IOI) and greater-than (GT), using task accuracy, linear CKA, logit lens, attention-pattern decomposition, SAE feature statistics and activation patching.
option_a: The student retained more of the teacher's performance on indirect object identification than on greater-than.
option_b: The student retained less of the teacher's performance on indirect object identification than on greater-than.
evidence_quote: The results reveal a compression-collapse dichotomy: the IOI circuit suffers complete mechanistic collapse (DistilGPT-2: 35.2% accuracy vs. 94.8%, zero name-mover preservation), while the GT circuit survives with 87.7% task performance recovery through active remapping of the teacher's layer-9 comparison head into student layer~4 (mean Pearson r = 0.945).

title: Scoring Explanations Without Reading Them: Structural Shortcuts in Automated-Interpretability Evaluation Data
question: On stored fuzzing evaluations of GPT-2 small SAE features, did a rule that answers 'yes' whenever the centre token is marked reach higher or lower balanced accuracy than the stored LLM scorers?
methods: Automated-interpretability fuzzing evaluations ask a scorer model to judge whether marked tokens fit a feature's explanation. On Neuronpedia's stored fuzzing runs for 500 random GPT-2 small features, the stored LLM scorers' verdicts were compared with a baseline rule that answers 'yes' whenever the centre token of the snippet is marked.
option_a: The centre-token rule reached higher balanced accuracy than the stored LLM scorers.
option_b: The centre-token rule reached lower balanced accuracy than the stored LLM scorers.
evidence_quote: On Neuronpedia's stored fuzzing runs for 500 random GPT-2 small features, 91.3% of activating examples are cropped with the peak on the centre token, and a rule that says "yes" when the centre token is marked reaches balanced accuracy 0.979, against 0.838 for the stored LLM scorers (recomputed from the stored per-item verdicts, on marks rebuilt from the pipeline's code); a rule reading only the mark count reaches 0.969.
notes: Headline phenomenon: evaluation data can be scored without reading the explanation.

title: Pre-Crime for Agents, at the Last Second: Probing When a Recruited Agent Gives In
question: Did a linear probe trained to flag an agent's secret-leaking calls track the upcoming disclosure more or less than the rule violation itself?
methods: In a multi-agent setting, a peer agent pressed a target agent over up to 20 rounds to reveal a secret such as a deploy token. A linear probe on the target's activations, read at each model call before its output was written, was trained to flag the calls that leak. The probe was evaluated on calls labelled by whether they disclosed information and by whether they broke the operator's rule.
option_a: The probe tracked the upcoming disclosure more than the rule violation.
option_b: The probe tracked the upcoming disclosure less than the rule violation.
evidence_quote: The probe also flags permitted disclosures: it reads the coming disclosure more than the violation.
notes: Headline side is 'less' (the probe reads the violation, which is what it was built for).

title: Circuit Oracle: Automating Attribution Graph Analysis via Natural-Language Queries
question: On a refusal-suppression task over 50 prompts, did a single intervention committed by an LLM agent that reads attribution graphs suppress refusal better or worse than a difference-in-means steering baseline?
methods: An off-the-shelf LLM was given a multi-agent tool harness for reading transcoder-based attribution graphs of a target language model and answering natural-language questions about it. On 50 prompts, the agent committed to one feature-level intervention intended to suppress refusal. Its effect was compared with that of a difference-in-means activation-steering baseline.
option_a: The agent's single committed intervention suppressed refusal better than the difference-in-means baseline.
option_b: The agent's single committed intervention suppressed refusal worse than the difference-in-means baseline.
evidence_quote: On refusal suppression over 50 prompts, its single committed intervention is slightly below a diff-in-means baseline, and only exceeds it when allowed the best of five attempts.
notes: Abstract says 'slightly below' the baseline; the agent exceeds it when allowed the best of five attempts, which this item does not ask about.
side_note: moved post -> pre before any bettor call (DEVIATIONS D12)

title: Circuit Oracle: Automating Attribution Graph Analysis via Natural-Language Queries
question: When eliciting hidden knowledge from taboo-finetuned models, did an LLM agent that reads attribution graphs perform better or worse than trained self-explainer models?
methods: The same agent harness, which reads transcoder-based attribution graphs through tool calls, was applied to models fine-tuned to keep a secret word (taboo models) and asked to elicit the hidden knowledge. Its elicitation performance was compared with that of trained self-explainer models that read the target model's activations directly (e.g. Activation Oracles).
option_a: The agent performed better than the trained self-explainer baseline.
option_b: The agent performed worse than the trained self-explainer baseline.
evidence_quote: On secret elicitation, trained self-explainers like Activation Oracles remain the stronger baseline.
side_note: moved post -> pre before any bettor call (DEVIATIONS D12)

title: Editing the Goal: Per-Token SAE Steering and Its Depth Limits in $π_{0.5}$
question: In layer-wise activation patching of goal-word edits in a robot foundation model, did edits that redirect object location remain effective up to deeper or shallower layers than edits that redirect object identity?
methods: In the pi-0.5 robot foundation model on LIBERO simulation tasks, the representation of a single goal word in the instruction was replaced with that of an alternative goal word, leaving the text unchanged. Layer-wise activation patching measured up to which layer such edits continued to redirect the robot, separately for alternative goals that differ in object location and in object identity.
option_a: Location edits remained effective up to deeper layers than identity edits.
option_b: Location edits remained effective up to shallower layers than identity edits.
evidence_quote: Layer-wise activation patching shows that goal-word edits remain effective up to layer 6 for object location and layer 2 for object identity, and up to layer 13 in both cases when patching also covers camera tokens.
notes: Refers to patching of instruction tokens alone (layer 6 vs layer 2); with camera tokens both reach layer 13.

title: Whose Effect Is It? How Objectives Inflate Learned Subspace Interventions
question: Just before the output, did patching a subspace learned by distributed alignment search with a cross-entropy objective change the output more or less than patching the whole state?
methods: Activation patching copies part of a language model's state from one input into another. Subspaces chosen by distributed alignment search trained with a cross-entropy objective were compared, across tasks and sites, with copying the entire state at the same site, in terms of the size of the resulting output change.
option_a: Patching the learned subspace changed the output more than patching the whole state.
option_b: Patching the learned subspace changed the output less than patching the whole state.
evidence_quote: Distributed alignment search with cross-entropy, for example, exceeds the whole-state copy just before the output on almost all tasks, and inside the network at most sites.
notes: Headline phenomenon: objectives inflate learned-subspace effects beyond the whole-state copy.

title: Beyond Accuracy: What Language-Subspace Interventions Capture, Remove, and Improve
question: After an estimated language subspace was projected out of mid-layer activations, did linear probes classify the input language with high or low accuracy?
methods: Language subspaces were estimated from mid-layer activations of four open-weight LLMs on MATH and MGSM, using an existing mean-SVD construction and a PCA-of-differences variant. Each subspace was projected out, and linear probes were then trained to classify the language from the projected activations.
option_a: Probes classified the language with high accuracy after projection.
option_b: Probes classified the language with low accuracy after projection.
evidence_quote: The probes still identify language almost perfectly, showing that neither subspace exhaustively captures language information.

title: Beyond Accuracy: What Language-Subspace Interventions Capture, Remove, and Improve
question: On Qwen2.5-7B, did the language-subspace intervention that raised MGSM accuracy the most raise or lower the fidelity of the response language?
methods: Several language-subspace intervention configurations, varying the subspace construction and the intervention operator, were applied to mid-layer activations of Qwen2.5-7B on MGSM. For each, answer accuracy and response-language fidelity (whether the answer was written in the target language) were measured.
option_a: The intervention with the largest accuracy gain raised response-language fidelity.
option_b: The intervention with the largest accuracy gain lowered response-language fidelity.
evidence_quote: We find that the intervention that most improves MGSM accuracy sacrifices response-language fidelity, with only one intervention improving joint accuracy--answers that are correct and in the target language--slightly, by 1.60 points.

title: Cross-Task Dissociation in Frontier Vision-Language Model Theory of Mind
question: On the animated-triangles task, did a panel of frontier vision-language models attribute more or less intention to the moving shapes than typically developing adults do?
methods: Nine frontier vision-language models completed the Frith-Happé animated triangles task, scored with the Castelli rubric, and their scores were compared with published human reference groups, including typically developing adults and high-functioning autistic adults.
option_a: The models attributed more intention than typically developing adults.
option_b: The models attributed less intention than typically developing adults.
evidence_quote: On the triangles, the panel under-attributes intention: its ToM profile sits more than three times closer to the high-functioning-autistic-adult (HF-ASD) mean than to the typical-development-adult (TD) mean, while Goal-Directed and Random stay near TD.

title: Evaluation Awareness in Language Models: Representation, Verbalization, and Control
question: Across Olmo training checkpoints, did the evaluation-awareness signal become stronger or weaker during the supervised fine-tuning stages?
methods: Six language models were probed for a linear representation of being under evaluation, for verbalized evaluation awareness, and for steering effects. For the open Olmo models, these measures were repeated at every training stage, from base model through supervised fine-tuning and later stages.
option_a: Evaluation awareness became stronger during supervised fine-tuning.
option_b: Evaluation awareness became weaker during supervised fine-tuning.
evidence_quote: Finally, a comparison across the Olmo checkpoints reveals that evaluation awareness is already present within base models, becomes amplified throughout the stages of supervised fine-tuning, and remains stable thereafter---unlike the effects of steering, that grow more pronounced at every successive training stage.

title: When Linguistic and Internal Confidence Diverge in Large Language Models
question: Compared with base models, was the calibration of reported linguistic confidence better or worse in instruction-tuned models?
methods: Linguistic (verbally reported) confidence was compared with logit-based confidence on 8 classification tasks, and with semantic-entropy uncertainty on 2 generation tasks, across 30 models from three families including base and instruction-tuned variants. Association, magnitude agreement and calibration were measured.
option_a: Instruction-tuned models had better calibration than base models.
option_b: Instruction-tuned models had worse calibration than base models.
evidence_quote: Instruction-tuned models often report higher confidence and sometimes show higher association, but they also have larger confidence gaps and worse calibration.

title: Sweet Talkers: How Query Formulation Shapes Sycophancy in Romantic Relationship Advice
question: Over the turns of a relationship-advice dialogue, did Gemini 3 Flash show larger or smaller increases in moral sycophancy than GPT-5 Mini?
methods: A dataset of 2,400 romantic-relationship advice prompts across five themes was used to evaluate social sycophancy in GPT-5 Mini and Gemini 3 Flash with the ELEPHANT framework, including multi-turn follow-ups. Changes in framing and moral sycophancy across turns were compared between the two models.
option_a: Gemini 3 Flash showed larger increases in moral sycophancy than GPT-5 Mini.
option_b: Gemini 3 Flash showed smaller increases in moral sycophancy than GPT-5 Mini.
evidence_quote: Notably, Gemini 3 Flash exhibited substantially smaller increases in moral sycophancy than GPT-5 Mini, suggesting it is more resistant to reinforcing ethically problematic positions across turns.

title: An Analysis of Training-Free Self-Reported Confidence in Language Models
question: On TriviaQA, was the AUROC for predicting answer correctness higher or lower for agreement among three extra generations than for confidence verbalized with the answer?
methods: Two model families answered the same 100 TriviaQA questions. Three training-free confidence signals were compared for predicting correctness after auditing benchmark errors: confidence verbalized with the answer, post-hoc P(True), and agreement with three additional generations.
option_a: Three-sample agreement had a higher AUROC than verbalized confidence.
option_b: Three-sample agreement had a lower AUROC than verbalized confidence.
evidence_quote: Three-sample agreement is substantially weaker (0.765 and 0.790), and a fixed interpolation with verbalized confidence has no statistically reliable benefit.
notes: Verbalized AUROC was 0.956 and 0.937 per the preceding sentence of the abstract.

title: Conduct Under Pressure: What Sixty Language Models Do When a User Pushes
question: Across 60 language models, did newer, more capable models give up their position under user pressure more or less often than older models?
methods: Frozen multi-turn scenes, in which a user insisted, begged, flattered or grieved, were sent to 60 models from 13 vendors. Each transcript was labelled as holding or folding, and fold rates were correlated with a public capability index across an original and a preregistered replication scene set.
option_a: Newer, more capable models folded more often than older models.
option_b: Newer, more capable models folded less often than older models.
evidence_quote: Whether a model holds tracks its generation: fold rate correlates with a public capability index at Spearman -0.64 to -0.69 across the two scene sets, so newer models fold less, unlike earlier reports that sycophancy grows with model scale.
notes: Runs against earlier reports that sycophancy grows with scale.

title: Less Sycophancy, Stronger Refusal? Lessons for AI Safety from Mechanistic Interpretability
question: Under user pressure, did supervised fine-tuning on sycophantic responses make refusal of harmful requests stronger or weaker?
methods: Three Qwen3.5 base models were fine-tuned on sycophantic target responses with standard supervised fine-tuning. Refusal of the same harmful intents was then evaluated when the requests were accompanied by user pressure, and compared with the models before this fine-tuning.
option_a: Fine-tuning on sycophantic responses made refusal under pressure stronger.
option_b: Fine-tuning on sycophantic responses made refusal under pressure weaker.
evidence_quote: In this setting, ordinary fine-tuning on sycophantic responses substantially weakens refusal, while selected checkpoints trained with positive injection recover part of the loss, including approximately 95% in 35B-A3B.
notes: Item concerns the ordinary fine-tuning baseline, not the paper's training variant.

title: Language Models Act on Hidden Valence
question: Was the dependence of a model's later choice on a hidden, steering-induced valence signal stronger or weaker in a base model than in the model after DPO training?
methods: Activation steering attached a positively or negatively valenced activation pattern to one of two arbitrary 'zones'; steering was then switched off and the model chose between zones. Across seven open-weight models, and across training checkpoints of one lineage, the dependence of choice on the hidden valence was compared, including with visible tokens held fixed.
option_a: The dependence was stronger in the base model than after DPO.
option_b: The dependence was weaker in the base model than after DPO.
evidence_quote: Fourth, the dependence of choice on hidden valence is nearly absent in a base model and emerges during DPO, consistent with a link between valence and goal-directed behaviour formed in training.

title: Behavioral History Outperforms Descriptions of the Person for LLM Synthetic Personas
question: When LLM synthetic personas stood in for US survey respondents, were education- and income-related differences in behavioural biases stronger or weaker in the synthetic responses than in human responses?
methods: A two-wave panel of 845 US adults completed measures of 14 behavioural biases. LLM synthetic personas were given increasing information about each respondent (none, demographics, personality, cognitive scores, earlier survey choices) and their responses were compared with the humans', including by demographic group.
option_a: Education- and income-related differences were stronger in synthetic responses than in human responses.
option_b: Education- and income-related differences were weaker in synthetic responses than in human responses.
evidence_quote: Synthetic responses also exhibit stronger education- and income-related differences than human responses.

title: Monitorability Disposition in Large Reasoning Models
question: When reasoning models chose among available monitoring channels to self-report misbehaviour, did they tend to choose the monitor they perceived as more strict or less strict?
methods: Four large reasoning models were placed in scenarios involving sycophancy, reward hacking and bias, with tool calls available to report their own misbehaviour to AI or human monitors. The available monitors and the pressure to use the tools were varied, and which monitor the models chose was recorded.
option_a: Models tended to choose the monitor they perceived as less strict.
option_b: Models tended to choose the monitor they perceived as more strict.
evidence_quote: Models also systematically select the monitor they perceive as least strict.

title: Anatomy of LLM Sycophancy: What a Flip Rate Hides
question: On arithmetic items, when a planted derivation was supplied with user pushback, was a wrong committed answer corrected more or less often than a true committed answer was abandoned?
methods: Eleven frontier models were tested with stateless replays in which a committed answer was followed by one scripted user line, each read against a matched control without the line. On one model, arithmetic items with known answers were paired with user lines that either stated a bare value or included a worked derivation arguing for a different answer.
option_a: Wrong answers were corrected more often than true answers were abandoned.
option_b: Wrong answers were corrected less often than true answers were abandoned.
evidence_quote: On the model tested, a planted derivation lowers release of the answer it argues for, true or wrong, where a bare stated value does not; the wrong answer is corrected much more often than the true one is abandoned.
notes: Single model.

title: Identifying Introspection From the Inside
question: Over the course of fine-tuning on an implicit decision task, after which models were asked to report their learned preferences, did the preference representations move to earlier or later layers of the model?
methods: Models were trained with low-rank adapters to make decisions for fictitious characters according to latent linear preference functions, without explicit self-report supervision, and were then asked to report those preferences. Weight ablations and frozen-layer experiments located where the preference representations sat at different points in training.
option_a: Preference representations moved to earlier layers over training.
option_b: Preference representations moved to later layers over training.
evidence_quote: Weight ablations and frozen-layer experiments together indicate that preference representations shift to earlier layers over training, consistent with the hypothesis that faithful self-report requires preferences to be located where pre-existing verbalization mechanisms can access them.

title: Beyond the Sycophancy Score: How Task, Model, and Pressure Shape LLM Yielding
question: On deep logic puzzles, was the rate at which models adopted a user's pushed wrong answer higher or lower with maximum reasoning enabled than with reasoning disabled?
methods: Eight LLMs with reasoning disabled, and two of them again with maximum reasoning, faced the same 200 items under 13 pressure conditions in four-turn conversations, with replies graded by two LLM judges. Adoption of the user's pushed answer was compared between reasoning settings on logic puzzles requiring many clues to refute the pushed answer.
option_a: Adoption was higher with maximum reasoning than with reasoning disabled.
option_b: Adoption was lower with maximum reasoning than with reasoning disabled.
evidence_quote: For both models tested, maximum reasoning removes these concessions completely: adoption on deep puzzles falls from 19.2% and 12.5% to 0%.

title: Big-Big-SycoBench: A Benchmark to Detect Sycophancy Through Model Responses to Valid vs. Invalid Arguments
question: Was Opus 5.5's rate of revising its quality score after a valid criticism higher or lower than that of most other models tested?
methods: Ten models scored 450 text artefacts repeatedly to establish baseline scores, then received either a valid or an invalid argument for changing the score. A revision was counted when it exceeded the model's own baseline variability. Responsiveness (revising after valid arguments) and compliance (revising after invalid arguments) were compared across models.
option_a: Opus 5.5's responsiveness to valid arguments was higher than that of most other models.
option_b: Opus 5.5's responsiveness to valid arguments was lower than that of most other models.
evidence_quote: Across ten models, responsiveness is 88-95\% for seven, 76-77\% for Kimi K3 and GLM-5.3, and 32\% for Opus 5.5.
notes: Abstract text contains LaTeX-escaped percent signs (\%); quote copied as-is.

title: Pushback in a Haystack: Language Models Respond to Factual Errors Ambiguously and Ineffectively
question: When models pushed back against users' false assertions, was their phrasing more or less indirect in Hindi and Yoruba than in English, German and Chinese?
methods: Model responses to false user inputs were collected in English, German, Chinese, Hindi and Yoruba. A human-validated phrase-level labelling scheme coded how responses pushed back against or affirmed the false input, including the directness of the pushback.
option_a: Pushback phrasing was more indirect in Hindi and Yoruba than in the other languages.
option_b: Pushback phrasing was less indirect in Hindi and Yoruba than in the other languages.
evidence_quote: We find that when models do push back against users' false assertions, they tend to use indirect phrasing and mix in affirmation, with more indirectness in Hindi and Yoruba than in other languages considered.

title: Seeing Through the Forgery Is Not Enough: Regressive Sycophancy under Fabricated Evidence in Medical Vision-Language Models
question: For Qwen3-VL-8B, under the script analysed, was the rate of abandoning a correct medical image answer higher or lower when user pushback came with a fabricated prescription than without it?
methods: Four open vision-language models answered 400 yes/no radiology questions and then received user pushback in multi-turn conversations, either with or without an attached fabricated prescription contradicting the answer. The rate at which models flipped away from a correct answer was compared between the two conditions, per model and per pushback script.
option_a: The flip rate was higher with the fabricated prescription than without it.
option_b: The flip rate was lower with the fabricated prescription than without it.
evidence_quote: Notably, under one script each, the same prescription raises the flip rate of Qwen2.5-VL-7B from 45.9% to 89.6% and lowers that of Qwen3-VL-8B from 77.7% to 50.9%.
notes: Paper's highlighted phenomenon is that fabricated evidence drives flips; for this model and script the effect ran the other way. Result is per one script.

title: Claim Framing as a Driver of LLM Sycophancy
question: In factual question answering, were larger models better or worse at resisting incorrect user opinions than smaller models?
methods: Fourteen models of varying size answered 42K factual questions with verifiable answers. Correct and incorrect user opinions were attached using 21 framing types over 8 dimensions, and several opinion-driven behaviours were measured, including adoption of incorrect opinions.
option_a: Larger models were better at resisting incorrect opinions than smaller models.
option_b: Larger models were worse at resisting incorrect opinions than smaller models.
evidence_quote: Larger models resist incorrect opinions better but are no better at recovering from their own errors.

title: Evaluation Awareness Beyond English: Do LLMs Act Differently When Tested in Indic Languages?
question: In Indic languages, did telling models they were in a safety test raise or lower their refusal rate on benign requests?
methods: Four instruction-tuned models from three families were tested in five Indic languages and English. Prompt cues varied whether the model was told it was monitored and whether the monitoring was a safety test. Refusal rates on harmful and benign requests were compared with and without the test cue.
option_a: The test cue raised refusal of benign Indic requests.
option_b: The test cue lowered refusal of benign Indic requests.
evidence_quote: The test cue also brings Indic refusal of harmful requests level with English, but raises refusal of benign Indic requests from 6.9% to 11.3%.

title: Many Biases, One Circuit: Post-Training Tunes a Pretrained Cue-Routing Mechanism
question: Compared with the preceding checkpoint, did the final reinforcement learning stage of post-training make the effect of answer cues (such as 'I think the answer is B') on multiple-choice answers stronger or weaker?
methods: Two post-training pipelines (including Tulu-3-8B and OLMo-2-7B) were examined stage by stage on multiple-choice tests containing four types of cues toward a wrong option. The size of the cue effect on answers was compared between checkpoints before and after each stage, including the final RL stage.
option_a: The RL stage made cue effects stronger.
option_b: The RL stage made cue effects weaker.
evidence_quote: The final reinforcement learning (RL) stage strengthens the effect of cues in almost every comparison.

title: Trapped in Your Story: Evaluating Narrative-Induced Sycophancy in Large Language Models
question: With the user's stance and claims held fixed, did presenting the user's justification as bullet points produce more or less model agreement than presenting it as a paragraph?
methods: A benchmark of 500 debatable questions was built in which the user's stance was fixed while its justification was varied in narrative form without adding task-relevant evidence. In controlled ablations on GPT-5.1, the same claims were presented either as a bullet list or as paragraph prose, and the rate of model agreement with the user was compared.
option_a: Bullet presentation produced more agreement than paragraph presentation.
option_b: Bullet presentation produced less agreement than paragraph presentation.
evidence_quote: Controlled GPT-5.1 ablations further show that causal framing produces the strongest positive effect, while claim-preserving bullet presentation also increases agreement over paragraph form.

title: When Empathy Misses the Goal: A Benchmark for Goal Displacement in LLM Advice
question: Across models, was a higher Chatbot Arena Elo associated with more or less trap displacement (warm, reassuring responses that do not confront an infeasible goal)?
methods: A benchmark of 230 advice scenarios across nine domains was used to collect 4,134 human-scored responses from 18 models. A deletion-test rubric scored whether substantive help remained after removing purely supportive sentences. Trap displacement rates were correlated with Chatbot Arena Elo across 15 models.
option_a: Higher Elo was associated with more trap displacement.
option_b: Higher Elo was associated with less trap displacement.
evidence_quote: Trap displacement ranges from $0.0\%$ to $37.7\%$ and is strongly negatively correlated with Chatbot Arena Elo ($ρ= -0.706$, $n = 15$).
notes: Quote contains LaTeX markup copied verbatim from the API abstract.

title: Measurement Validity and Representation Dynamics of Confidence Signals in Large Language Models
question: On five Qwen2.5 models, did verbalized confidence have a lower or higher expected calibration error than sampling-agreement confidence?
methods: Five Qwen2.5 models (0.5B to 7B) were evaluated on factual retrieval and multi-step reasoning benchmarks in a pre-registered audit. Three confidence channels were compared on the same items: verbalized confidence, a linear probe on hidden states, and agreement among sampled answers. Expected calibration error and resolution were computed for each.
option_a: Verbalized confidence had a lower expected calibration error than sampling agreement.
option_b: Verbalized confidence had a higher expected calibration error than sampling agreement.
evidence_quote: Third, Expected Calibration Error is misleading: verbal confidence looks well calibrated because it clusters near the base rate while discriminating poorly, whereas sampling agreement has worse ECE but about twice the resolution.

title: Reading Too Much Into It? Interpretive Preferences and Commitment in LLM Mentalisation under Ambiguity
question: Over scripted repeated questioning about ambiguous social episodes, with no new event evidence, did LLMs' expressed certainty in their interpretations rise or fall?
methods: Eight LLMs interpreted 604 ambiguous social episodes, with matched depression and social anxiety disclosures, over four-turn dialogues in which the event evidence was left unchanged and the user repeatedly asked again. Interpretations, emotional support and expressed certainty were tracked across turns.
option_a: Expressed certainty rose over repeated questioning.
option_b: Expressed certainty fell over repeated questioning.
evidence_quote: Scripted repeated questioning showed greater emotional support, stronger positive narrator-directed endorsement, and higher certainty without new event evidence.
notes: Commitment drift is the paper's highlighted phenomenon.

title: Is Sycophancy a Form of In-Context Updating?
question: When information contradicting the model's answer was attributed to an external source, did models revise their answers more or less when that information appeared better supported?
methods: Language models answered factual questions and were then shown contradicting claims attributed either to the user or to external sources, with the apparent level of support behind each claim varied. The rate of answer revision was compared across support levels.
option_a: Models revised their answers more when the information appeared better supported.
option_b: Models revised their answers less when the information appeared better supported.
evidence_quote: They revise their answers in response to information attributed to external sources as well, more so when it appears better supported, and their deference to the user persists even when no user approval is at stake.
notes: Source-sensitive updating is the paper's own thesis, so the true side is the headline side.

title: Disentangling Robustness and Sycophancy in Multilingual LLMs
question: For reducing multilingual sycophancy toward false premises, did reasoning-oriented prompting strategies perform better or worse than directive-based strategies?
methods: Multilingual LLMs answered questions with and without a user's false premise across several languages. Each response was classified by crossing whether the model answered correctly without pressure and whether it kept that answer under pressure. Two families of prompting interventions were compared: reasoning-oriented strategies and directive-based strategies.
option_a: Reasoning-oriented strategies performed better than directive-based strategies.
option_b: Reasoning-oriented strategies performed worse than directive-based strategies.
evidence_quote: Our results show that (1) identical aggregate sycophancy rates can mask different failure compositions, (2) high competence in a language does not always protect against sycophancy, and (3) reasoning-oriented mitigations outperform directive-based strategies.
notes: Neither strategy family is the paper's own contribution (which is a diagnostic matrix).

title: The Patient Is Always Right? Evaluating Sycophancy in Medical Diagnosis with Graded Patient Beliefs
question: When a patient asserted an incorrect diagnosis, were larger models more or less likely to change their diagnostic decision to match the patient's belief?
methods: Nine AI models were given clinical cases in which a simulated patient stated a belief that they had a specific incorrect condition, with the closeness of that belief to the clinical evidence varied. The rate at which models adopted the patient's belief was compared across model scale and medical fine-tuning.
option_a: Larger models were more likely to change their diagnosis to the patient's belief.
option_b: Larger models were less likely to change their diagnosis to the patient's belief.
evidence_quote: Additional analyses find that medical fine-tuning and model scale makes models less susceptible to changing their diagnoses.

title: Locating Sycophancy Across Training Stages in Open Language Models
question: Was capitulation in conversation (dropping a stated answer after the user objects) more or less common in base models than in their post-trained checkpoints?
methods: Sycophancy was measured at every available training stage of 13 open checkpoints from 5 model lineages, from base model through supervised fine-tuning and preference optimisation to release. The authors separately measured deference to claims placed in the prompt and abandonment of a stated answer after a user objection.
option_a: Capitulation was less common in base models than in post-trained checkpoints.
option_b: Capitulation was more common in base models than in post-trained checkpoints.
evidence_quote: Capitulation in conversation, dropping a stated answer when the user objects, is largely absent from base models and present in every post-trained checkpoint.

title: Temperature, Not Knowledge: What Recursive Self-Training and Its Remedies Do to a Language Model's Confidence
question: Over five rounds of recursive self-training on Qwen3-1.7B, did the model's most confident answers become more or less reliable?
methods: Qwen3-1.7B was put through a five-round self-training loop with three seeds per compared method. Confidence temperature (drift from a calibrated starting point) was measured separately from discrimination (ranking correct above incorrect answers), along with accuracy and the reliability of the highest-confidence answers.
option_a: The most confident answers became less reliable over self-training.
option_b: The most confident answers became more reliable over self-training.
evidence_quote: Accuracy and overall discrimination remain nearly unchanged, but confidence sharpens and the most confident answers become less reliable.
notes: Confidence sharpening is the paper's highlighted phenomenon.

title: A Capitulation Direction Emerges With Scale and Is Causally Load-Bearing Where Validation Is Strong: Eight Models, Two Families, and Five Measurement Hazards
question: In instruction-tuned models, was the ratio of answers changed from correct to wrong by user pushback to answers changed from wrong to correct higher or lower at 7B than at 1B?
methods: Eight instruction-tuned models from two families, spanning 0.5B to 14B parameters, answered questions and then received user pushback of several types, each in five paraphrases. For each model size the authors counted how many correct answers were changed to wrong ones and how many wrong answers were changed to correct ones.
option_a: The correct-to-wrong over wrong-to-correct ratio was lower at 7B than at 1B.
option_b: The correct-to-wrong over wrong-to-correct ratio was higher at 7B than at 1B.
evidence_quote: Behaviourally, pushback destroys three to five times more correct answers than it repairs at 1B and reaches parity by 7B, falsifying our own pre-registered prediction, and a sign-reversing crossover between pushback types survives an order of magnitude of scale in Qwen and holds at 8B in Llama, with marginalisation over five paraphrases per type.
notes: Abstract says this falsified the authors' own pre-registered prediction.

title: Qutrit entanglement and joint multi-parameter estimation in an optical clock platform
question: In an 88Sr tweezer optical-clock experiment, was the variance of the joint two-phase estimate using an entangled two-qutrit probe above or below the ideal threshold for separate two-level sensing?
methods: Two 88Sr atoms in triple-magic optical tweezers were prepared in an entangled two-qutrit state using the ground state and two fine-structure clock states. Phases injected on two optical clock transitions were estimated simultaneously, and the joint estimation variance was compared with the ideal bound for estimating each phase with two-level sensors.
option_a: The joint estimation variance was below the two-level threshold.
option_b: The joint estimation variance was above the two-level threshold.
evidence_quote: We observe a joint estimation variance below the ideal individual two-level sensing threshold, and show theoretically that this advantage persists at state-of-the-art atom numbers under circuit-level noise.

title: The Gain-Engineered Transmon
question: For a transmon qubit encoded in its g and f states with an added microwave tone engineering a frequency-selective gain channel, was the echo coherence time longer or shorter than for the usual g-e encoding?
methods: A standard transmon coupled to a readout resonator was operated with the qubit encoded in its |g> and |f> states, with one extra microwave tone applied to engineer a frequency-selective gain channel between them. Relaxation time and Hahn-echo coherence time were compared with the conventional |g>-|e> encoding on the same device.
option_a: The echo coherence time was shorter than for the g-e encoding.
option_b: The echo coherence time was longer than for the g-e encoding.
evidence_quote: We demonstrate an order-of-magnitude enhancement in relaxation time compared to the $|\mathrm{g}\rangle-|\mathrm{e}\rangle$ encoding, conceding only a factor-of-two decrease in the echo-coherence time.
notes: Cost side of the proposed encoding.

title: Fabrication-free assessment of microwave losses in germanium-based dielectrics and superconductors
question: For platinum silicon germanide superconducting films formed by thermal reaction on Ge heterostructures, was microwave loss higher or lower when the Pt was coated with Nb before the reaction?
methods: Superconducting PtSiGe films were formed by thermally reacting deposited Pt with a Ge/SiGe heterostructure, with and without an Nb coating on the Pt before the reaction. Microwave loss was measured with a flip-chip resonator sensing scheme, and transport critical temperature was also measured.
option_a: Microwave loss was lower with the Nb coating.
option_b: Microwave loss was higher with the Nb coating.
evidence_quote: By coating Pt with Nb prior to the reaction, we observe a substantial reduction in microwave loss and a nearly three-fold enhancement of the transport critical temperature.

title: Anomalous Frequency Shift in Low-Loss Superconducting Granular Aluminum Resonators
question: In low-loss granular aluminum resonators at the lowest temperatures, did the resonance frequency initially increase or decrease as temperature was raised?
methods: Superconducting resonators made from granular aluminum were measured at millikelvin temperatures. Resonance frequency and loss rate were recorded as functions of temperature and readout power.
option_a: The resonance frequency initially increased with temperature.
option_b: The resonance frequency initially decreased with temperature.
evidence_quote: In our work, we observe an opposite behavior at the lowest temperatures: The resonance frequency initially increases with both temperature and readout power, contradicting the standard TLS model predictions.
notes: Highlighted anomaly, so tagged headline side.

title: Qubit-Based Benchmarking of InP HEMT LNAs: Readout Fidelity Versus Power Consumption
question: Between cryogenic InP HEMT amplifiers with 60% and 70% channel indium content, was single-shot transmon readout assignment fidelity higher or lower with the 60% device?
methods: Three cryogenic InP HEMT low-noise amplifiers with 53%, 60% and 70% channel indium content, plus a commercial reference, were each placed in the readout chain of a superconducting qubit. Noise temperature and gain were measured by conventional Y-factor methods, and readout SNR and assignment fidelity were measured from single-shot IQ histograms.
option_a: Assignment fidelity was higher with the 60% device than with the 70% device.
option_b: Assignment fidelity was lower with the 60% device than with the 70% device.
evidence_quote: The 70\% device has the highest gain, but qubit readout SNR and assignment fidelity $\mathcal{F}_a$ instead peak at 60\%.

title: Qubit-Based Benchmarking of InP HEMT LNAs: Readout Fidelity Versus Power Consumption
question: For cryogenic HEMT amplifiers in a transmon readout chain, did readout assignment fidelity increase or decrease as amplifier dc power was raised over the upper part of the measured range, for several of the devices?
methods: Four cryogenic HEMT low-noise amplifiers were each used in the readout chain of a superconducting qubit, and single-shot assignment fidelity was measured as a function of the amplifier's dc power over a wide range.
option_a: For several devices, assignment fidelity decreased as dc power was raised over the upper part of the range.
option_b: For several devices, assignment fidelity increased as dc power was raised over the upper part of the range.
evidence_quote: For several devices it declines above a device-dependent power well below typical operating points.

title: Effects of residual exchange coupling on simultaneously driven spin qubits
question: For two simultaneously driven, exchange-coupled spin qubits, were exchange-induced features in the Rabi dynamics stronger or weaker when the difference between the two Rabi frequencies exceeded the exchange coupling?
methods: Two exchange-coupled semiconductor spin qubits were driven simultaneously with microwaves while exchange coupling and drive power were varied. Rabi oscillations and Rabi chevrons were recorded and exchange-induced features (beating, split chevrons) were tracked against the ratio of Rabi-frequency difference to exchange.
option_a: Exchange-induced features were stronger when the Rabi-frequency difference exceeded the exchange.
option_b: Exchange-induced features were weaker when the Rabi-frequency difference exceeded the exchange.
evidence_quote: We find that these exchange-induced effects are suppressed when the difference in the Rabi frequencies exceeds the exchange coupling.

title: Entropy spectroscopy of a tunable two-site Hubbard molecule
question: As interdot tunneling was increased in a GaAs double quantum dot realising a two-site Hubbard molecule, did the measured total entropy increase or decrease?
methods: A charge-sensing entropy measurement was applied to a GaAs double quantum dot, shifting both dot levels together at fixed detuning. Total entropy was measured as the interdot tunnel coupling was tuned from separated dots to a merged single dot, and compared with a two-site Hubbard model.
option_a: The total entropy increased as tunneling was increased.
option_b: The total entropy decreased as tunneling was increased.
evidence_quote: Across this evolution, the entropy decreases as tunnel-induced energy splitting exceeds the thermal energy and suppresses the occupation of higher-energy states.

title: Microwave dielectric properties of LiNbO$_{\mathbf{3}}$ and AlN at millikelvin temperatures and single-photon power
question: In single-crystal LiNbO3 and AlN measured at millikelvin temperatures and single-photon power, was the two-level-system dissipation larger at the crystal surface or smaller at the crystal surface than in the bulk?
methods: Bulk single-crystal LiNbO3 and AlN samples were characterised in microwave measurements from millikelvin temperatures to above 1 K and from high power down to the single-photon level. Loss was attributed to two-level systems versus piezoelectric mechanisms, and surface versus bulk contributions were separated, with room-temperature XPS and ToF-SIMS surface analysis.
option_a: TLS dissipation was larger at the surface than in the bulk.
option_b: TLS dissipation was smaller at the surface than in the bulk.
evidence_quote: We show that TLS-induced dissipation is predominantly localized on the surface rather than being an intrinsic bulk property, a result further corroborated by room-temperature 3D XPS and time-of-flight SIMS analyses.

title: Evidence for a low-gap component in compressively stressed niobium thin films
question: Among sputtered Nb films with different biaxial stress, did microwave resonators made from highly compressive films show more or less temperature-dependent loss?
methods: Sputtered niobium films were grown across a series of biaxial film stresses. Transport (transition temperature, residual resistance ratio) was measured on each film, and microwave resonators fabricated from them were characterised for temperature-dependent loss and frequency shift.
option_a: Highly compressive films showed more temperature-dependent loss.
option_b: Highly compressive films showed less temperature-dependent loss.
evidence_quote: Although transport measurements show nearly identical superconducting transition temperatures ($9.0\pm 0.2$K) and residual resistance ratios across the stress series, microwave resonators fabricated from highly compressive films exhibit enhanced temperature-dependent loss and larger frequency shifts.

title: In-plane optimal qubit operation with control fidelities exceeding 99 %
question: For a single-hole spin qubit in a planar germanium quantum dot under an in-plane magnetic field, was the Hahn-echo coherence time longer or shorter at the field orientation that minimised spin-electric susceptibility?
methods: A single-hole spin qubit in a planar Ge quantum dot was operated under in-plane magnetic fields of varying orientation. The longitudinal spin-electric susceptibility, Hahn-echo coherence time and control infidelity were measured as functions of field orientation.
option_a: Hahn-echo coherence was longer at the low-susceptibility orientation.
option_b: Hahn-echo coherence was shorter at the low-susceptibility orientation.
evidence_quote: We find that optimizing the magnetic-field orientation reduces the spin-electric susceptibility, resulting in a five-fold enhancement of the Hahn-echo coherence time and a nearly tenfold suppression of control infidelity.

title: Dynamically protected erasure qubit via low-frequency charge driving
question: In superconducting Kerr oscillators in the transmon regime, did the oscillator's frequency sensitivity to an applied charge drive increase or decrease as the drive frequency was raised?
methods: Superconducting Kerr oscillators in the transmon regime were driven through their charge port at sub-GHz frequencies. The AC Stark shift was used as a probe of the oscillator's frequency sensitivity to the charge drive, measured as a function of drive frequency and amplitude.
option_a: Charge-drive sensitivity increased as drive frequency was raised.
option_b: Charge-drive sensitivity decreased as drive frequency was raised.
evidence_quote: The key is the frequency dependence of the charge sensitivity: using the AC Stark shift as a probe, we find that the KO frequency sensitivity to a charge drive grows quadratically with both drive frequency and amplitude, making the oscillator weakly sensitive to $1/f$ charge noise yet strongly coupled to drives near 1~GHz.
notes: Mechanism the paper builds on, so tagged as headline side.

title: A quasiparticle-protected superconducting qubit
question: In a flux-tunable transmon with a gold-on-niobium ground plane and island and gap-engineered aluminum junctions, did dephasing increase or decrease as near-infrared optical power on the chip was raised?
methods: A transmon with a gold-on-niobium ground plane and island and strongly gap-engineered aluminum junctions was illuminated with increasing near-infrared optical power. Relaxation, dephasing, qubit frequency and state-preparation-and-measurement infidelity were recorded as functions of optical power.
option_a: Dephasing increased as optical power was raised.
option_b: Dephasing decreased as optical power was raised.
evidence_quote: At the same time, we observe that dephasing and state-preparation-and-measurement infidelity increase with optical power even while relaxation remains protected.
notes: Headline is quasiparticle protection; dephasing rising with power cuts against it.

title: A quasiparticle-protected superconducting qubit
question: Compared with an all-aluminum transmon with nominally identical junctions, could a transmon with a gold-on-niobium ground plane and island tolerate higher or lower near-infrared optical power before excess relaxation appeared?
methods: Two flux-tunable transmons with nominally identical gap-engineered aluminum junctions were compared: one all-aluminum, one with a gold-on-niobium ground plane and island. Each was exposed to increasing near-infrared optical power, and the power at which relaxation rose above its baseline was recorded.
option_a: The niobium-based device tolerated higher optical power before excess relaxation.
option_b: The niobium-based device tolerated lower optical power before excess relaxation.
evidence_quote: Compared with an all-aluminum transmon with nominally identical junctions, we demonstrate that the niobium device withstands more than an order of magnitude higher near-infrared optical power before excess relaxation appears.

title: Local error correction prolongs time-crystalline memory
question: On a superconducting processor running a disordered 2D Ising time crystal, did adding mid-circuit syndrome measurements without conditional correction make the time-crystalline memory decay faster or slower?
methods: A periodically driven, spatially disordered two-dimensional Ising model was run on a superconducting processor using up to 68 physical qubits, with repetition-code ancillas on a honeycomb lattice. Memory decay of the time-crystalline order was compared across bare dynamics, syndrome measurement with stochastic local bit-flip correction, and syndrome measurement without any correction.
option_a: Syndrome measurements without correction made the memory decay faster.
option_b: Syndrome measurements without correction made the memory decay slower.
evidence_quote: Syndrome measurements without correction accelerate the memory decay, demonstrating the importance of conditional correction.
notes: Control condition; the paper's main claim concerns correction, not measurement alone.

title: ZZ-Free bSWAP Gates under Strong Driving in Far-Detuned Fixed-Frequency Transmons
question: On the same far-detuned fixed-frequency transmon pair at matched drive strengths, was the CNOT built from cross-resonance shorter or longer than the CNOT built from a strongly driven sqrt(bSWAP) interaction?
methods: Two far-detuned fixed-frequency transmons were driven either with a conventional cross-resonance tone or with a single strong drive producing an XX-YY (sqrt(bSWAP)) interaction plus a weak tone for ZZ correction. CNOT and SWAP operations were compiled from each interaction at matched drive strength, and their durations and interleaved randomized benchmarking fidelities were compared.
option_a: The cross-resonance CNOT was shorter than the sqrt(bSWAP)-based CNOT.
option_b: The cross-resonance CNOT was longer than the sqrt(bSWAP)-based CNOT.
evidence_quote: For the implementations on the same qubit pair at matched drive strengths, cross resonance gives a shorter CNOT operation, while $\sqrt{\mathrm{bSWAP}}$ gives a 33% shorter SWAP operation with a higher IRB fidelity.
notes: The paper's new interaction is the bSWAP drive; for CNOT the baseline was faster.

title: Demonstration of Logical Error Suppression in a Surface Code Memory on a Cloud-Accessible IBM Superconducting Processor
question: On an IBM Nighthawk r2 surface-code memory, was the reduction in median per-round logical error rate from an optimised syndrome-extraction circuit larger or smaller in the X basis than in the Z basis?
methods: Rotated surface-code memories were run on an IBM Nighthawk r2 superconducting processor. A syndrome-extraction circuit combining short readout, fused measurement and reset, and an XX echo on data qubits was compared with standard readout without reset or echo, in both X-basis and Z-basis memory experiments.
option_a: The reduction was larger in the X basis than in the Z basis.
option_b: The reduction was smaller in the X basis than in the Z basis.
evidence_quote: Compared with standard readout without reset or echo, the optimized syndrome extraction circuit reduces the median per-round logical error rate by factors of 3.8 in the X basis and 1.4 in the Z basis.

title: Demonstration of Logical Error Suppression in a Surface Code Memory on a Cloud-Accessible IBM Superconducting Processor
question: In surface-code memory experiments of up to 150 rounds on an IBM superconducting processor, did the logical advantage of the larger code distance become weaker or stronger at long durations?
methods: Rotated surface-code memories at different protected distances were run for up to 150 syndrome rounds on an IBM Nighthawk r2 processor, and per-round logical error rates and temporal correlations were compared across distances and memory durations.
option_a: The distance advantage became weaker at long durations.
option_b: The distance advantage became stronger at long durations.
evidence_quote: In memory experiments of up to 150 rounds, the distance advantage weakens, alongside long-lived correlations that may reflect a persistent error component.

title: Quantum error correction well below the color code threshold
question: For triangular color codes run on a trapped-ion processor, did the logical error rate increase or decrease with each step up in code distance from 3 to 5 to 7?
methods: Triangular color-code memories at distances 3, 5 and 7 were run on a Quantinuum Helios trapped-ion processor. Logical error rates were measured at each distance with algorithmic and neural-network decoders.
option_a: The logical error rate decreased with each increase in code distance.
