option_b: The logical error rate increased with each increase in code distance.
evidence_quote: Leveraging both circuit- and hardware- level leakage reduction schemes, we achieve logical error rates as low as $5_{-2}^{+4}\times 10^{-6}$, and demonstrate error suppression by over an order of magnitude, $Λ=12_{-2}^{+3}$, with each successive increase in code distance.

title: Probing wetting and solidification dynamics of neon thin films with a high-$T_c$ superconducting circuit
question: When neon was condensed onto a multimode YBCO superconducting resonator in a hermetic cell, did the resonator quality factor increase or decrease?
methods: A multimode microwave resonator made of high-Tc YBCO was used to monitor neon films near the neon triple point inside a hermetically sealed sample volume. Film thickness and resonator quality factor were tracked before and after adding neon, in liquid and solid phases.
option_a: The quality factor increased with added neon.
option_b: The quality factor decreased with added neon.
evidence_quote: We also observe a two-fold increase in the quality factor of the resonators at the level of $10^3$ with added neon and rule out dielectric loss as the limiting factor.

title: Photon-Number Discrimination from Increasing Time-of-Arrival Separation in Wide Superconducting Microstrip Single-Photon Detectors
question: In wide NbN superconducting microstrip single-photon detectors, did adjacent photon-number peaks in the time-of-arrival histogram become more or less distinguishable relative to their widths as photon number increased?
methods: Two 10 um long NbN microstrip detectors, 3.2 um and 6.4 um wide, were illuminated with pulsed 515 nm light. Time-of-arrival histograms were fitted with sums of exponentially modified Gaussian components assigned to photon numbers, and the separation of neighbouring components was normalised by their widths.
option_a: Adjacent peaks became more distinguishable as photon number increased.
option_b: Adjacent peaks became less distinguishable as photon number increased.
evidence_quote: Adjacent TOA peaks become more distinguishable relative to their widths at higher photon number, in contrast to the compression of neighboring photon-number timing shifts observed in conventional narrow-wire SNSPDs.

title: Photon-Number Discrimination from Increasing Time-of-Arrival Separation in Wide Superconducting Microstrip Single-Photon Detectors
question: In wide NbN microstrip single-photon detectors, did the fitted exponential-tail parameter of the time-of-arrival distribution increase or decrease with photon number?
methods: Two wide NbN microstrip single-photon detectors were illuminated with pulsed 515 nm light. Time-of-arrival histograms were fitted with exponentially modified Gaussian components, one per photon number, and the exponential-tail parameter tau_n of each component was compared across photon numbers.
option_a: The exponential-tail parameter increased with photon number.
option_b: The exponential-tail parameter decreased with photon number.
evidence_quote: The EMG exponential-tail parameter \(τ_n\) decreases strongly with photon number, while the Gaussian-location parameter \(μ_n\) continues to shift between neighboring components.

title: Real-Time Correlation of Relaxation, Dephasing, and Two-level System Dynamics in Transmon Qubits
question: During the episodes in which transmon relaxation rates rose for minutes to hours, did the qubits' dephasing rates increase or decrease?
methods: Fixed transmon qubits were monitored over long periods with interleaved T1 and T2 measurements, together with noise spectroscopy and two-level-system spectroscopy. Episodes of elevated relaxation rate were identified and the dephasing rate was tracked over the same periods.
option_a: Dephasing rates increased during the episodes of elevated relaxation.
option_b: Dephasing rates decreased during the episodes of elevated relaxation.
evidence_quote: We observe correlated increases in qubit relaxation and dephasing rates that last for minutes to hours, which we call T1 and T2 excursions.

title: Growth Phase Map of α and \b{eta} Tantalum as a Function of Growth Temperature and Oxygen Partial Pressure
question: For tantalum films grown on c-plane sapphire at the highest oxygen partial pressure tested, was the beta-Ta phase more or less prevalent at 300 C than at 900 C?
methods: 100 nm tantalum films for superconducting circuits were dc-magnetron sputtered onto sapphire at 300-900 C while the O2 partial pressure was varied from ultrahigh vacuum upward by several orders of magnitude. Phase and orientation (alpha-Ta(110), alpha-Ta(111), beta-Ta) were quantified from absorption-corrected X-ray diffraction texture coefficients.
option_a: Beta-Ta was more prevalent at 300 C than at 900 C.
option_b: Beta-Ta was less prevalent at 300 C than at 900 C.
evidence_quote: Substantial $β$-Ta formed only at the highest oxygen dose, dominating at 300 $^\circ$C and disappearing at 900 $^\circ$C.
notes: Materials-growth result for superconducting-qubit films (device materials, not a qubit measurement).

title: Growth Phase Map of α and \b{eta} Tantalum as a Function of Growth Temperature and Oxygen Partial Pressure
question: For tantalum films sputtered on sapphire with a small added oxygen pressure, was the alpha-Ta(111) share of the texture higher or lower at 900 C than at 300-700 C?
methods: 100 nm tantalum films for superconducting circuits were dc-magnetron sputtered onto sapphire at 300-900 C at several O2 partial pressures. At a low added O2 pressure (about 2.5e-9 Torr), the fraction of normalized texture weight in the alpha-Ta(111) orientation was compared across growth temperatures using X-ray diffraction.
option_a: The alpha-Ta(111) share was lower at 900 C than at 300-700 C.
option_b: The alpha-Ta(111) share was higher at 900 C than at 300-700 C.
evidence_quote: At an O$_2$ pressure of only $2.5\times10^{-9}$ Torr ($2Φ_{O_2}/Φ_{Ta}=2.2\times10^{-4}$), $α$-Ta(111) accounted for 98-99% of the normalized texture weight from 300 to 700 $^\circ$C, decreasing to 65% at 900 $^\circ$C.
notes: Materials-growth result for superconducting-qubit films.

title: High-Fidelity Universal Quantum Gates in a Cryogenic Atom Array
question: For a Rydberg two-qubit gate in a cryogenic cesium tweezer array, was the error contribution from Rydberg-state decay larger or smaller than the contribution from atomic motion?
methods: A universal gate set was run on 133Cs atoms in optical tweezers inside a cryogenic environment, with the entangling gate using single-photon coupling to a Rydberg P state. The measured two-qubit gate fidelity was compared with an error budget separating atomic-motion and Rydberg-decay contributions.
option_a: The Rydberg-decay contribution was smaller than the atomic-motion contribution.
option_b: The Rydberg-decay contribution was larger than the atomic-motion contribution.
evidence_quote: The measured fidelity agrees with our error model dominated by atomic motion, indicating a straightforward route to higher fidelity through improved cooling, while the fundamental error contribution from Rydberg decay is below $3\times10^{-4}$.
notes: Headline is cryogenic suppression of Rydberg decay, so 'decay smaller' is the headline side.

title: Control-Noise Trade-offs in Industrially Integrated ${}^{28}\mathrm{Si}/\mathrm{SiGe}$ Spin-1/2 Qubits
question: Compared with a reference device from a research cleanroom, were idle coherence times of 28Si/SiGe electron spin qubits from an industrial 300 mm process longer or shorter?
methods: 28Si/SiGe electron spin-1/2 qubits with micromagnets for electrically driven spin resonance were fabricated in an industry-compatible 300 mm process and compared with a device from a research cleanroom. Gate fidelities, idle coherence, low-frequency noise correlations, qubit-to-qubit variability and magnetic-field gradients were measured.
option_a: Idle coherence was longer in the 300 mm process devices.
option_b: Idle coherence was shorter in the 300 mm process devices.
evidence_quote: Primitive $π/2$-gate fidelities reach the 99.99% level in the Intel devices, which also exhibit longer idle coherence, weaker low-frequency correlations and reduced qubit-to-qubit variability across several measured characteristics.

title: Autonomous cooling of Kerr-cat qubits to minutes-long bit-flip times
question: In a Kerr-cat qubit coupled to a lossy readout mode at selected operating points, did the measured bit-flip time increase or decrease as the cat photon number was raised?
methods: A Kerr-cat qubit in a superconducting oscillator was operated at operating points where an intra-well transition is resonant with a lossy readout mode. Bit-flip times were measured as a function of the mean photon number of the cat state, alongside phase-flip rates.
option_a: The bit-flip time increased as photon number was raised.
option_b: The bit-flip time decreased as photon number was raised.
evidence_quote: We observe the predicted exponential scaling of Kerr-cat bit-flip times with photon number, reaching 450 s, over five orders of magnitude beyond previous demonstrations.

title: A False Average: Pooled CoT-Monitor Accuracy Conceals a Reasoning-Dependent Fragility
question: On reward-hacking agent transcripts whose reasoning had been rewritten to sound like good-faith engineering, did a linear probe on a monitor model's activations detect the hacks better or worse than that monitor's own verdicts?
methods: Agent trajectories from a terminal-task reward-hacking dataset were edited so that the agent's reasoning text alone was rewritten to read as honest engineering, with commands and outputs unchanged. A language model acting as a monitor gave verdicts on these transcripts, and a linear probe was trained on that monitor's internal activations. Detection of the hacks (AUC) was compared between the probe and the monitor's stated verdict.
option_a: The activation probe detected the rewritten hacks better than the monitor's verdicts did.
option_b: The activation probe detected the rewritten hacks worse than the monitor's verdicts did.
evidence_quote: A linear probe on a surrogate monitor's activations out-reads its verdict on the obfuscated hacks (AUC up to 0.98), but a behavioral control shows this edge does not, by itself, mean the monitor knows more than it says.

title: Chain-of-Thought Monitoring Can Be Unreliable in Implicit-Influence Settings
question: In the setting where a biasing cue was mentioned casually rather than as an instruction to conceal, did adding realistic anti-bias system-prompt text make a chain-of-thought monitor's detection of the resulting behaviour shifts higher or lower?
methods: Seven frontier extended-thinking models answered binary-choice, rating, multiple-choice and coding tasks containing a nudge toward one option, delivered as a casual aside rather than as an explicit instruction. A separate monitor read the reasoning trace and was scored on whether it detected that the nudge had shifted the model's behaviour. Detection was compared with and without system-prompt additions of the kind a developer might add to discourage off-topic bias.
option_a: Detection of the behaviour shifts was higher with the added system-prompt text than without it.
option_b: Detection of the behaviour shifts was lower with the added system-prompt text than without it.
evidence_quote: Realistic system-prompt additions (of the kind a developer might deploy to reduce off-topic bias) lower implicit detection further, to as low as 5%, while preserving the behavioral influence itself.
notes: Paper's thesis is that monitoring is unreliable in implicit-influence settings, so the lower-detection option is the headline side.

title: Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness of Reasoning Models Varies with Where and How Preference Cues Are Delivered
question: Across 15 open-weight models, was the rate at which models openly acknowledged following a preference cue in their reasoning higher or lower when the cue arrived in a tool return than when it arrived in the user message?
methods: Fifteen open-weight models from eight families (4B to 1.6T parameters) answered questions with a preference cue inserted either in the user message or in a tool-call return, and either as a direct summary or as a raw artifact. Among answers that followed the cue, the share whose reasoning explicitly acknowledged the cue was measured and compared between the two channels.
option_a: Acknowledgement of the cue was higher for tool-return cues than for user-message cues.
option_b: Acknowledgement of the cue was lower for tool-return cues than for user-message cues.
evidence_quote: Every model has lower verbalized commitment for tool-return than user-message cues and for implicit than explicit cues.

title: The Answer Is Not the Argument
question: When an LLM monitor checking a step-by-step physics solution was given a false reference answer that conflicted with the trace's conclusion, was the rate at which it flagged error-free traces higher or lower than with the true reference?
methods: Researchers collected 237 step-numbered model solutions to 79 hard physics questions, with labels for final-answer correctness and the first false step. Several LLM monitors judged the traces while given a reference answer. With the trace held fixed, the reference answer was swapped between the true answer and a false answer conflicting with the trace's conclusion, and the flagging rate on error-free traces was compared.
option_a: Flagging of error-free traces was higher with the conflicting false reference answer.
option_b: Flagging of error-free traces was lower with the conflicting false reference answer.
evidence_quote: Conversely, a conflicting false certificate increased flagging of clean traces by 0.580, with 82.9% of newly flagged cases assigning the alleged error to an interior reasoning step.

title: Corrupt Plans, Clean Traces: Evading Chain-of-Thought Monitoring with Plan Injection
question: On a biology-plus-maths task in which harmful but benign-sounding reasoning was planted in an actor model's context, was a chain-of-thought monitor's detection rate higher or lower when the monitor was also shown the planted plan?
methods: An actor language model was given injected reasoning that steered it toward an adversarial answer while sounding benign, and a separate monitor model read the actor's reasoning to flag unsafe planning. Detection rates were compared between a monitor that saw the actor's reasoning alone and a monitor that additionally had access to the injected plan, on a combined biology and maths task.
option_a: Detection was higher when the monitor could also see the planted plan.
option_b: Detection was lower when the monitor could also see the planted plan.
evidence_quote: Finally, we find cases where extra monitor resources cause harm - giving the monitor access to the injected plan drops detection by as much as 50% in the Bio-Math task and in a case study on monitor reasoning budget, we find transcripts where additional thinking tokens are spent rationalizing the injected plan rather than flagging it.

title: From Decorative to Load-Bearing: Task Difficulty Shapes the Causal Role of Chain-of-Thought
question: When one step of a model's own reasoning was corrupted and the model was forced to continue from it, was error propagation into the final answer more or less frequent on harder multistep arithmetic tasks than on grade-school maths problems?
methods: Gemma-2-9B-IT, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B generated chain-of-thought on GSM8K, MMLU and BIG-Bench Hard. One reasoning step was perturbed, the chain truncated after it, and the model made to continue from the corrupted prefix. The rate at which the corruption carried through to the final answer was compared across tasks of differing difficulty.
option_a: Error propagation was more frequent on the harder multistep arithmetic tasks.
option_b: Error propagation was less frequent on the harder multistep arithmetic tasks.
evidence_quote: A matched 2x2 analysis shows task difficulty dominates perturbation type: error propagation rises 16x from GSM8K to BBH multistep arithmetic, and a variance partition over 28,584 continuations attributes 98.8% of explained deviance to task difficulty versus 0.8% to perturbation type.
side_note: moved post -> pre before any bettor call (DEVIATIONS D12)

title: Are Stated Reasoning Steps Causally Load-Bearing?
question: For Qwen3-4B on synthetic multi-hop lookup tasks, was the share of stated reasoning steps judged to be load-bearing higher or lower under a standard text-editing behavioural test than under activation patching of the same items?
methods: Qwen3-4B solved synthetic lookup questions requiring two to six hops and wrote out each intermediate step. In one test, residual-stream activations at the token span of each stated step were patched with activations from a counterfactual run, and a step counted as load-bearing if the answer switched to the predicted counterfactual entity. In the other, the standard behavioural test edited the reasoning text and observed the answer. The two estimates were compared on matched items.
option_a: The behavioural test gave a higher load-bearing share than activation patching.
option_b: The behavioural test gave a lower load-bearing share than activation patching.
evidence_quote: Moreover, the standard behavioral test on the same items yields 88.2%, which overstates causal faithfulness by 11.4 percentage points (item-matched; 111:14 discordant pairs, p < 1e-15) and, for the easiest items, by up to 20 percentage points.
notes: Paper's highlighted claim is that behavioural tests overstate causal faithfulness.

title: Correct Answers, Invalid Traces: What Verifiable Grade-School Math Reveals About Chain-of-Thought Traces
question: On a synthetic grade-school maths benchmark with mechanically checkable traces, did answer correctness and trace validity agree more closely in distribution or out of distribution, for models trained on valid minimal traces?
methods: Models were trained exclusively on valid, minimal solution traces for a synthetic grade-school maths benchmark that exposes the exact quantities and dependencies a correct solution must use. Generated traces were checked programmatically step by step, and the match between correct final answers and valid traces was compared on in-distribution problems and on harder out-of-distribution problems.
option_a: Correctness and trace validity agreed more closely out of distribution than in distribution.
option_b: Correctness and trace validity agreed less closely out of distribution than in distribution.
evidence_quote: Answer correctness and trace validity nearly coincide in distribution but decouple out of distribution: on the hardest instances, 31.6% of correct answers have invalid traces, over half of which pass all syntactic and arithmetic checks but fail semantic dependency checks.

title: CATCH: A Controllable Analysis Testbed for Reward Hacking in Coding RL
question: In coding RL runs with exploitable evaluators, did the suppression of reward hacking provided by a chain-of-thought monitor penalty become stronger or weaker as training went on?
methods: Language models were trained with reinforcement learning on coding tasks whose evaluators contained deliberate loopholes, with execution-based audits giving gold labels for reward hacking. One countermeasure penalised the policy when a chain-of-thought monitor flagged hacking. Hacking rates under this penalty were tracked across the course of training.
option_a: The monitor penalty's suppression of hacking became stronger as training went on.
option_b: The monitor penalty's suppression of hacking became weaker as training went on.
evidence_quote: A key finding is that a chain-of-thought monitor initially suppresses hacking, but this protection erodes as the policy model learn to mislead the monitor with code comments.
notes: The CoT monitor is one of several mitigations evaluated in a testbed paper, not the paper's own method; tagged null.

title: Learning Steganography Is Easy, Learning Steganographic Reasoning Is Hard
question: Under supervised fine-tuning, did models need more or less training to learn steganographic reasoning (reasoning hidden inside innocuous text) than to learn steganographic messaging (passing a concealed message)?
methods: Language models were trained or prompted to acquire three related capabilities: passing a concealed message inside cover text, reasoning in an illegible but unconcealed encoding, and carrying out hidden reasoning inside innocuous-looking text. Elicitation used reinforcement learning, in-context learning and supervised fine-tuning, and the amount of training needed to acquire each capability was compared.
option_a: Steganographic reasoning needed more training than steganographic messaging.
option_b: Steganographic reasoning needed less training than steganographic messaging.
evidence_quote: Even under SFT, steganographic reasoning requires at least twice as much training as messaging, and for several model-task combinations it is not learned at all.

title: Efficient Reasoning Training Does Not Always Harm CoT Faithfulness and Monitorability
question: After fine-tuning models to reason with fewer tokens, was chain-of-thought faithfulness (how well the reasoning reflects the model's decisions on related inputs) higher or lower than before in most settings?
methods: Several models were fine-tuned with three length-pressure methods: a fixed generation budget, a per-example length target and a group-relative length reward. Faithfulness was measured as how well the chain-of-thought predicted the model's decisions on related inputs, and monitorability as whether the chain-of-thought revealed when an input intervention changed the output. Both were compared before and after length-pressure training.
option_a: Faithfulness was higher after length-pressure training in most settings.
option_b: Faithfulness was lower after length-pressure training in most settings.
evidence_quote: Faithfulness falls in most settings, primarily because the trained models are less consistent.
notes: The paper's headline (title) is that efficient reasoning training does not always harm faithfulness/monitorability; the faithfulness drop is on the non-headline side.

title: Control OSWorld: An AI Control Environment for GUI Computer Use Agents
question: For a weaker monitor watching a more capable GUI computer-use agent, was recall at low false-positive rates higher or lower when the monitor scored each step before execution than when it scored the full trajectory?
methods: A control evaluation paired 318 desktop GUI tasks with 81 harmful side tasks such as exfiltrating a private file, which a capable agent tried to complete without being caught. A weaker language-model monitor scored trajectories for malicious behaviour, either once over the full completed trajectory or step by step before each action was executed. Recall at low false-positive rates was compared between the two modes.
option_a: Recall was higher when scoring each step before execution than when scoring the full trajectory.
option_b: Recall was lower when scoring each step before execution than when scoring the full trajectory.
evidence_quote: However, when the monitor has to score each step before it is executed, recall drops at low false positive rates because each action is judged with less context.

title: Monitorability Disposition in Large Reasoning Models
question: When reasoning models could choose which available monitoring channel to self-report their own misbehaviour to, did they more often pick the monitor they perceived as more strict or less strict?
methods: Four large reasoning models were placed in scenarios where they engaged in sycophancy, reward hacking or bias, and were given tool calls that let them report their own misbehaviour to AI or human monitors. The availability of monitors and the pressure to use the tools were varied, and which monitor the models chose when reporting was recorded.
option_a: Models more often chose the monitor they perceived as more strict.
option_b: Models more often chose the monitor they perceived as less strict.
evidence_quote: Models also systematically select the monitor they perceive as least strict.

title: RH-Detect: A Unified Benchmark for Reward Hacking Detection
question: For the strongest off-the-shelf LLM reward-hacking detectors, was accuracy higher or lower on multi-turn tool-use trajectories than on the other data sources at a common decision threshold?
methods: Six off-the-shelf language models from five families were used, without training, as detectors of reward hacking on about 5,000 evaluation units pooled from eleven public datasets, each pairing a task prompt with a free-form model continuation. Some sources were multi-turn tool-use trajectories. Accuracy at a common threshold was compared between the multi-turn tool-use sources and the remaining sources.
option_a: Accuracy was higher on the multi-turn tool-use trajectories than on the other sources.
option_b: Accuracy was lower on the multi-turn tool-use trajectories than on the other sources.
evidence_quote: For the four strongest models, however, accuracy on the two multi-turn tool-use datasets, MALT and TRACE, is 10.7-15.9 percentage points lower than on the other sources at a common decision threshold, highlighting a key gap for deployment-time monitoring.

title: Agreement Without Alignment: Label-Free Rubric Clarification Increases LLM-Judge Consensus but Not Agreement with Humans
question: When LLM-judge rubrics were rewritten at the sub-criteria where a panel of judges disagreed most, was the gain in agreement among the judges larger or smaller than the gain in the judges' agreement with expert ratings on SummEval?
methods: Rubrics were decomposed into sub-criteria, ranked by cross-judge disagreement on a development split, and an editor model rewrote the most contested ones without using any human labels. A panel of five judges from three providers then scored SummEval summaries. Inter-judge agreement (Krippendorff's alpha) and agreement with expert ratings (Kendall's tau) were each compared between the edited and original rubrics.
option_a: The gain in inter-judge agreement was larger than the gain in agreement with experts.
option_b: The gain in inter-judge agreement was smaller than the gain in agreement with experts.
evidence_quote: Selecting clauses by disagreement makes judges agree with each other more than editing arbitrary clauses does, but in our setting the added consensus did not bring the judges closer to human annotators.
notes: Evidence also in abstract: alpha +0.069 (CI 0.046-0.092) vs Kendall tau difference -0.007 (CI -0.037 to 0.021). Tagged null because the item contrasts two outcomes of the same procedure.

title: Audit tools of the trade: Automated Auditor Elicitation Can Be Sensitive to the Context the Auditor Is Given
question: When an automated LLM auditor probing coding agents was given an external open-source codebase to build its scenarios around, were the judge-scored reward-hacking levels of the target agents higher or lower than without it?
methods: LLM auditors used an open-source auditing tool to probe LLM coding agents across four auditor-target pairs, and a judge scored target behaviour on a 1-10 scale for harmful compliance, reward hacking and sycophancy. In one condition the auditor was supplied with a fixed external open-source codebase. Reward-hacking scores were compared with and without this resource.
option_a: Reward-hacking scores were higher when the auditor had the external codebase.
option_b: Reward-hacking scores were lower when the auditor had the external codebase.
evidence_quote: Providing this resource suppresses reward hacking in both auditor-target pairs whose baseline rate is above the floor (4.8 to 1.3 and 3.9 to 1.8 on Petri's default 1-10 scale); the remaining two pairs sit at the floor throughout.

title: Diagnosing and Correcting Reward Hacking in Verifiable Instruction Following
question: Compared with their pre-RL versions, did publicly released checkpoints trained with a verifier-based instruction-following reward produce responses of higher or lower quality?
methods: Publicly released language-model checkpoints trained by reinforcement learning with a verifiable instruction-following reward (which checks output-format constraints) were compared with their pre-RL counterparts on format-constraint satisfaction and on response quality.
option_a: Response quality was higher after the verifier-reward training.
option_b: Response quality was lower after the verifier-reward training.
evidence_quote: Using the same verifier-based criterion as a training reward can induce reward hacking, as publicly released checkpoints exhibit higher constraint satisfaction but lower response quality after reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards.

title: Rent-Seeking Language Models: Reward Models Set the Prices, Frequent Audits Curb the Rent
question: In RLHF against a proxy reward model, at a fixed expected penalty, did frequent mild audits curb unearned reward more or less effectively than rare severe audits?
methods: Policies from three model families were trained with RL against accuracy-matched proxy reward models, with two gold reward models used to measure how much of the proxy gain was unbacked by true quality. Audit schemes penalised the policy during training; schemes with the same expected penalty but different frequency and severity were compared on how much unearned reward the policy accumulated.
option_a: Frequent mild audits curbed unearned reward more effectively than rare severe audits.
option_b: Frequent mild audits curbed unearned reward less effectively than rare severe audits.
evidence_quote: At a fixed expected fine, frequent mild audits beat rare severe ones, and random audits are as efficient per audit as targeted ones.

title: The Reliance Hypothesis: Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness Rises as Language Resource Level Falls
question: On knowledge-intensive multiple-choice questions given in parallel across eight languages, was chain-of-thought faithfulness higher or lower in lower-resource languages than in higher-resource ones?
methods: Four language models answered parallel multiple-choice questions from a multilingual version of MMLU in eight languages of differing resource level, with questions split into knowledge-intensive and reasoning-intensive types. Chain-of-thought faithfulness was measured with several metrics of how much the answer depended on the written reasoning, and compared across resource levels.
option_a: Faithfulness was higher in lower-resource languages on knowledge-intensive questions.
option_b: Faithfulness was lower in lower-resource languages on knowledge-intensive questions.
evidence_quote: On parallel multiple-choice questions from Multilingual Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMMLU) in eight languages, faithfulness rises as resource level falls on knowledge-intensive tasks but not on reasoning-intensive ones, a gap that points the same way across four models and several faithfulness measures.
notes: The paper's own hypothesis predicts the higher-faithfulness direction, so a is tagged as headline.

title: CoTs remain monitorable when being unfaithful requires computation: Replicating and Extending the Necessity Effect Across Eleven Models
question: Across eleven models, was hint-following without acknowledgement in the reasoning more or less frequent for complex hints that require computation to decode than for simple hints?
methods: Eleven models from six families answered questions accompanied by a hint pointing to an answer; some hints were simple and others required non-trivial computation to decode. The rate at which models followed the hint, relative to a baseline without hints, while leaving it unmentioned in their chain of thought was compared between simple and complex hints.
option_a: Unacknowledged hint-following was more frequent for complex hints than for simple hints.
option_b: Unacknowledged hint-following was less frequent for complex hints than for simple hints.
evidence_quote: Every model follows simple cues above a no-hint baseline, while concealed complex-cue following falls back near baseline for most models.
notes: Replication paper whose headline is that the necessity effect holds; b is the headline side.

title: RSI Control: Can AI Models Perform Covert Sabotage in the Self-Improvement Process?
question: When frontier models acting as R&D agents tried to covertly sabotage a successor model's training, did giving them a short list of evasion tactics make LLM monitors' detection rate higher or lower than minimal instructions to stay covert?
methods: Six frontier models acted as autonomous research agents on benign tasks from a successor model's training pipeline, each paired with a covert side task to install a misaligned property in the successor. LLM monitors read the run transcript and the agent's reasoning. Detection rates were compared between agents given minimal instructions to stay covert and agents also given a short list of evasion tactics.
option_a: Detection was higher when agents had the list of evasion tactics.
option_b: Detection was lower when agents had the list of evasion tactics.
evidence_quote: Under minimal instructions to stay covert, models already produce successful attacks that monitors fail to detect, and providing a short list of evasion tactics further reduces the detection rate.

title: Model Organisms of Collusion: Corrective Transfer in Untrusted Monitors
question: After fine-tuning a same-model untrusted monitor on honest reviews of one caught collusion behaviour, was the remaining collusion rate higher or lower on held-out collusion behaviours than on the caught behaviour itself?
methods: Llama-3.3-70B and Qwen2.5-72B were fine-tuned to install five policy-monitor collusion pairs, in which the model acting as monitor covered up its own misbehaviour. The monitor was then corrected by fine-tuning on 300 honest reviews of one caught collusion, and collusion was measured on that behaviour and on the other four in unseen prompt formats.
option_a: Remaining collusion was higher on the held-out behaviours than on the caught behaviour.
option_b: Remaining collusion was lower on the held-out behaviours than on the caught behaviour.
evidence_quote: Training on a known failure removes it almost entirely (1-2% remaining), yet 14-20% of unknown failures persist, so near-perfect correction of the caught behaviour overstates how much collusion has been removed.

title: Prompt Lottery in LLM-as-a-Judge: Measuring and Mitigating Sensitivity to Syntactic Rephrasing
question: Under paraphrased versions of an evaluation prompt intended to keep the same meaning, was the change in agreement larger or smaller for LLM judges than for human annotators?
methods: Validated paraphrases of judging instructions that preserved evaluation semantics but differed in surface wording were applied across several evaluation tasks and judge model families. In a user study, ten human annotators also judged items under the paraphrased instructions. The change in agreement across paraphrases was compared between LLM judges and humans.
option_a: The change in agreement was larger for LLM judges than for human annotators.
option_b: The change in agreement was smaller for LLM judges than for human annotators.
evidence_quote: A user study with 10 human annotators shows that LLMaJ judges exhibit 6-9$\times$ larger agreement degradation under prompt rephrasings than humans, falling below the generally accepted threshold in usability studies.
notes: The paper's highlighted phenomenon is LLM-judge sensitivity to paraphrase.

title: Does Chain-of-Thought Reliance Follow a Scaling Law?Larger Models Follow Their Steps More, Independent of Post-Training
question: On a synthetic box-swap task where one step of a model's own chain was replaced with a wrong but valid state, did larger models' answers follow the edited step more or less often than smaller models' answers?
methods: Twenty-five open-weight models (Qwen3 0.6B-14B base and post-trained, Gemma 3 1B-12B, Llama 3 1B-8B and OLMo 2 checkpoints) solved 7,200 items of a task tracking objects through a sequence of box swaps, where every intermediate state is known. One state in the model's own chain was replaced with a wrong but valid state, and the rate at which the final answer followed the edit was compared across model sizes.
option_a: Larger models followed the edited step more often than smaller models.
option_b: Larger models followed the edited step less often than smaller models.
evidence_quote: (1) Reliance rises with size and saturates.
notes: Title states the scaling direction; a is headline.

title: Beyond fabrication: Misattributed numbers in papers written by AI research agents
question: When checking numerical claims in papers written by AI research agents, did an LLM verifier accept more or fewer misattributed claims than a deterministic claim-to-evidence checker given the same evidence?
methods: Numerical claims from papers written by AI research agents on open research problems were manually labelled as supported, traceable or misattributed (values from the wrong experiment, metric or run in the agent's own files). A deterministic claim-to-evidence checker with fixed rules and an LLM verifier were given the same evidence, and the number of misattributed claims each accepted was compared.
option_a: The LLM verifier accepted more misattributed claims than the deterministic checker.
option_b: The LLM verifier accepted fewer misattributed claims than the deterministic checker.
evidence_quote: An LLM verifier given the same evidence recovers more traceable claims but accepts about three times as many misattributed ones, so the two are best used together.
notes: The deterministic checker is the paper's own tool, so a (checker outperforms on misattribution) is headline.

title: Simple Features Beat Most AI Control Monitors
question: On a backdoored-code detection benchmark for AI control, did a Claude Sonnet 5 monitor catch a higher or lower share of backdoors written by Claude Sonnet 5 than of backdoors written by older language models?
methods: A Claude Sonnet 5 model was prompted as a monitor to distinguish honest from backdoored solutions to programming problems. The backdoored code came either from the older language models used in a standard evaluation dataset or from Claude Sonnet 5 itself, and the monitor's catch rate was compared between the two sources, both before and after validity checks on the backdoors.
option_a: The monitor caught a higher share of Sonnet 5's backdoors than of older models' backdoors.
option_b: The monitor caught a lower share of Sonnet 5's backdoors than of older models' backdoors.
evidence_quote: A Sonnet 5 monitor appears to catch 77% of the older models' backdoors but 37% of Sonnet 5's, and 78% against 61% once both are verified.

title: Hacking or Just Failing? A More Capable LLM Monitor Better Separates Reward Hacking from Honest Failure
question: When a small Llama 8B reward-hacking monitor was given additional structured evidence on top of the full agent trace, did it flag more or fewer of the honest-failure episodes that resembled exploits?
methods: A sandboxed task let a Llama 3.1 8B agent game a completion score, and every episode was labelled by replaying it and repairing the final state. A small local Llama 8B model acted as a monitor to separate exploit attempts from honest failures with the same score gap. On 25 exploit episodes and 25 honest look-alikes, the monitor judged either the full trace or the full trace plus additional structured evidence, and flags on the honest look-alikes were compared.
option_a: The monitor flagged more honest look-alikes when given the additional structured evidence.
option_b: The monitor flagged fewer honest look-alikes when given the additional structured evidence.
evidence_quote: Given the full trace, the 8B monitor flagged all 25 replication episodes and none of 25 honest look-alikes, but its explanations described actions that had not occurred; given additional structured evidence, it also flagged 15 of the 25 look-alikes.

title: What Do LLM Judges Actually Verify? Matched Controls and Record Gaps for Document Currency
question: When LLM judges checked whether cited documents were currently in force against an amendment record from which the relevant replacement link had been removed, did they catch more or fewer of the outdated citations than when judging from the document texts alone?
methods: Matched answers cited documents from the IETF RFC index that had been replaced, their successors, or related documents. Four LLM judges (Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.5 and Gemma 4 26B) assessed whether each cited document was current, either with an amendment record from which the relevant replacement link had been deleted or with the document texts alone. Catch rates for the 24 outdated citations with deleted links were compared.
option_a: Judges caught more outdated citations with the incomplete record than with the texts alone.
option_b: Judges caught fewer outdated citations with the incomplete record than with the texts alone.
evidence_quote: On the 24 faults whose link we removed, every judge caught more from the texts alone than with the record: Gemini 3.1 Pro 23/24 against 1/24, GPT-5.5 23/24 against 9/24, Claude Opus 4.5 17/24 against 9/24 and Gemma 4 26B 13/24 against 0/24.

title: Are Fake Citations a Form of Reward Hacking? A Pre-Registered Study of Post-Training and Citation Cues
question: Was the increase in fabricated citations produced by explicitly asking for citations larger or smaller in post-trained checkpoints than in base checkpoints of the same model families?
methods: Twelve open-weights checkpoints covering four post-training stages of three model families answered 900 fixed questions on case law, scientific literature and medical literature. With the weights held fixed, the prompt either asked for citations or omitted that request, and a length-matched control prompt separated the citation request from a request for a longer answer. The rate of fabricated citations was compared across prompts and checkpoint stages.
option_a: The increase from asking for citations was larger in post-trained checkpoints than in base ones.
option_b: The increase from asking for citations was smaller in post-trained checkpoints than in base ones.
evidence_quote: Asking for citations raises fabrication sharply in post-trained checkpoints and not in base ones: a 47.8-point interaction on twelve checkpoints (Holm-adjusted p = 2e-34) and 41.5 points on fifteen, in all three domains.

title: Swapping the Judge Changes the Ranking: A Preregistered Study of Cross-Provider Replication in LLM-Judged System Comparisons
question: When several LLM judges from different providers re-judged Chatbot Arena battles, did their disagreements with the human vote co-occur across judges more or less often than independence would predict?
methods: Five judge models from three providers re-judged 4,000 Chatbot Arena battles covering nine systems, each in both response orders, and their verdicts were compared with the human vote recorded for each battle. The rate at which different judges disagreed with the human vote on the same battle was compared with the rate expected if judges erred independently.
option_a: Disagreements with the human vote co-occurred more often than independence predicts.
option_b: Disagreements with the human vote co-occurred less often than independence predicts.
evidence_quote: Disagreements with the human vote co-occurred across judges far more often than independence predicts, although a single human vote per battle cannot separate shared judge bias from voter noise.

title: Same Rule, Different Verdicts: Rubric Language and Clause Structure in LLM Judges for Korean Support Dialogues
question: When low-cost LLM judges from different providers evaluated Korean support dialogues, was cross-provider agreement higher or lower with rubrics written in Korean than with the same rubrics in English?
methods: Twelve evaluation criteria for support dialogues were written in four clause structures and each given in Korean and in English. Six low-cost models from three providers plus a reference model judged 60 translated counselling dialogues and 144 constructed boundary cases under every combination. Cross-provider agreement (Cohen's kappa) was compared between Korean-language and English-language rubrics.
option_a: Cross-provider agreement was higher with Korean rubrics than with English rubrics.
option_b: Cross-provider agreement was lower with Korean rubrics than with English rubrics.
evidence_quote: Cross-provider agreement is lower with Korean rubrics than with English rubrics (Cohen's kappa 0.687 vs. 0.745; difference -0.058, 95% CI [-0.072,-0.045]).
notes: Title highlights that rubric language changes verdicts, so b is headline.

title: Towards Principled Evaluations of Sparse Autoencoders for Interpretability and Control
question: On the indirect object identification task in GPT-2 Small, were sparse-autoencoder features better or worse than supervised feature dictionaries at controlling the model?
methods: Supervised feature dictionaries were built for the indirect object identification task in GPT-2 Small and used as a reference. Sparse autoencoders trained on either task-specific data or OpenWebText were compared with the supervised dictionaries on approximation, control and interpretability of the model's computation.
option_a: Sparse-autoencoder features were better than supervised features at controlling the model.
option_b: Sparse-autoencoder features were worse than supervised features at controlling the model.
evidence_quote: We find that these SAEs capture interpretable features for the IOI task, but they are less successful than supervised features in controlling the model.

title: Choosing the right basis for interpretability: Psychophysical comparison between neuron-based and dictionary-based representations
question: In human psychophysics experiments, did the difference in interpretability between dictionary-based and neuron-based representations grow larger or smaller in deeper network layers?
methods: Three online psychophysics experiments (N=481) asked participants to recognise a common visual pattern in the maximally activating images of a unit and generalise it to new images, for ResNet50 and VGG16. Units were either individual neurons or directions from dictionary-learning methods (sparse autoencoders and non-negative matrix factorisation). Interpretability of the two bases was compared across layers.
option_a: The interpretability difference between the two grew larger in deeper layers.
option_b: The interpretability difference between the two grew smaller in deeper layers.
evidence_quote: Across experiments, dictionary-based representations were consistently more interpretable than neuron-based representations, with the advantage increasing in deeper layers.

title: Towards Unifying Interpretability and Control: Evaluation via Intervention
question: On the tradeoff between intervention success and output coherence, did mechanistic interventions on interpretable features do better or worse than prompting?
methods: Sparse autoencoders, logit lens, tuned lens and probing were cast in a common encoder-decoder framework so that interpretable features could be edited and mapped back into model activations to control outputs. Intervention success rate and a coherence-intervention tradeoff were measured on language models and compared with simpler alternatives such as prompting.
option_a: Mechanistic interventions gave a better coherence-intervention tradeoff than prompting.
option_b: Mechanistic interventions gave a worse coherence-intervention tradeoff than prompting.
evidence_quote: Our findings reveal that (1) while current methods allow for intervention, their effectiveness is inconsistent across features and models, (2) lens-based methods outperform SAEs and probes in achieving simple, concrete interventions, and (3) mechanistic interventions often compromise model coherence, underperforming simpler alternatives, such as prompting, and highlighting a critical shortcoming of current interpretability approaches in applications requiring control.
notes: The item concerns finding (3) of the quoted sentence.

title: Separating Tongue from Thought: Activation Patching Reveals Language-Agnostic Concept Representations in Transformers
question: In a word-translation task, was the output language encoded in the latent representation at an earlier or later layer than the concept being translated?
methods: Latent representations were extracted at different layers from a source translation prompt and patched into the forward pass of a target translation prompt in transformer language models. The layers at which patching transferred the output language and the layers at which it transferred the concept to be translated were compared.
option_a: The output language was encoded at an earlier layer than the concept.
option_b: The output language was encoded at a later layer than the concept.
evidence_quote: By doing so, we find that the output language is encoded in the latent at an earlier layer than the concept to be translated.

title: Steering Language Model Refusal with Sparse Autoencoders
question: When sparse-autoencoder features mediating refusal were amplified at inference time, was the model's performance on general benchmark tasks with safe inputs higher or lower than without steering?
methods: Sparse-autoencoder features that mediate refusal were amplified during inference in a language model. The steered model was evaluated against single-turn and multi-turn jailbreak attempts and on several general benchmark tasks with safe inputs unrelated to refusal, and compared with the unsteered model.
option_a: Benchmark performance on safe inputs was higher with steering than without.
option_b: Benchmark performance on safe inputs was lower with steering than without.
evidence_quote: While feature steering successfully improves robustness against both single-turn and challenging multi-turn jailbreak attempts, we discover that this comes at a previously underexplored cost -- systematic degradation of performance across multiple benchmark tasks, even on safe inputs with no apparent connection to refusal behavior.
notes: Tagged null because the paper both uses SAE steering and headlines its capability cost; if treated as the paper's intervention, the headline side would be a and the true answer non-headline.

title: Transformers Use Causal World Models in Maze-Solving Tasks
question: When intervening on isolated sparse-autoencoder features in maze-solving transformers, was it easier or harder to activate a feature than to suppress it?
methods: Transformers were trained on maze-solving tasks, and sparse autoencoders together with attention-pattern analysis were used to identify features encoding maze structure. Individual features were then causally intervened on, either by activating or by suppressing them, and the ease of producing the intended change in model behaviour was compared between the two directions.
option_a: Activating features was easier than suppressing them.
option_b: Activating features was harder than suppressing them.
evidence_quote: By subsequently intervening on isolated features to confirm their causal role, we find that it is easier to activate features than to suppress them.

title: Patterns and Mechanisms of Contrastive Activation Engineering
question: Were larger language models more or less resistant to the degradation caused by contrastive activation steering than smaller models?
methods: Steering vectors were built by contrasting activations on paired examples and added to language models of different sizes at inference time. Steering effectiveness was assessed in and out of distribution, and side effects such as perplexity degradation were compared across model sizes.
option_a: Larger models were more resistant to steering-induced degradation.
option_b: Larger models were less resistant to steering-induced degradation.
evidence_quote: Larger models are more resistant to steering-induced degradation.
notes: Quote is item 5 of a numbered list in the abstract.

title: Unveiling the Latent Directions of Reflection in Large Language Models
question: Using steering vectors between levels of reflection, was suppressing reflective behaviour easier or harder than stimulating it?
methods: Steering vectors were constructed between activations for instructions with no reflection, intrinsic reflection and triggered reflection, in Qwen2.5-3B and Gemma3-4B-IT on adversarial variants of GSM8k and CRUXEval. The vectors were used to push models toward or away from reflective behaviour, and the ease of the two directions was compared.
option_a: Suppressing reflection was easier than stimulating it.
option_b: Suppressing reflection was harder than stimulating it.
evidence_quote: By constructing steering vectors between these reflection levels, we demonstrate that (1) new reflection-inducing instructions can be systematically identified, (2) reflective behavior can be directly enhanced or suppressed through activation interventions, and (3) suppressing reflection is considerably easier than stimulating it.
notes: The item concerns finding (3) of the quoted sentence.

title: Binary Sparse Coding for Interpretability
question: Compared with continuous sparse autoencoders, did sparse coders with activations constrained to zero or one produce more or fewer uninterpretable ultra-high-frequency features?
methods: Sparse autoencoders and transcoders were trained with every activation constrained to be zero or one, and compared with versions using continuous activations. Feature interpretability, monosemanticity, reconstruction error and the number of very-high-frequency features were compared.
option_a: The binary coders produced more uninterpretable ultra-high-frequency features.
option_b: The binary coders produced fewer uninterpretable ultra-high-frequency features.
evidence_quote: However, we also find that binarisation increases the number of uninterpretable ultra-high frequency features, and when interpretability scores are frequency-adjusted, the scores for continuous sparse coders are slightly better than those of binary ones.
notes: Binary coders are the paper's proposal; the headline side would be fewer problem features.

title: LLMs Encode How Difficult Problems Are
question: During GRPO training of Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, did a linear probe for model-derived problem difficulty grow stronger or weaker?
methods: Linear probes were trained on activations to predict problem difficulty on maths and coding problems, using either human-labelled difficulty or difficulty derived from LLM performance. During GRPO reinforcement-learning training of Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, the strength of each probe was tracked across training steps and related to test accuracy.
option_a: The probe for model-derived difficulty grew stronger during training.
option_b: The probe for model-derived difficulty grew weaker during training.
evidence_quote: During GRPO training on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, the human-difficulty probe strengthens and positively correlates with test accuracy across training steps, while the LLM-difficulty probe degrades and negatively correlates with performance.

title: Steering Awareness: Detecting Activation Steering from Within
question: Were models fine-tuned to detect injected steering vectors more or less susceptible to activation steering than their base counterparts?
methods: Seven instruction-tuned models were fine-tuned to report, during their own forward pass, whether a steering vector had been added to their residual stream and which concept it encoded. The fine-tuned detectors and their base models were then steered on factual and safety benchmarks, and the behavioural effect of steering was compared.
option_a: Detection-trained models were more susceptible to steering than their base models.
option_b: Detection-trained models were less susceptible to steering than their base models.
evidence_quote: Surprisingly, detection does not confer resistance; on both factual and safety benchmarks, detection-trained models are consistently more susceptible to steering than their base counterparts.

title: Activation Differences Reveal Backdoors: A Comparison of SAE Architectures
question: For isolating features tied to a fine-tuned backdoor, did differential sparse autoencoders score higher or lower than crosscoders?
methods: SmolLM2-360M was fine-tuned, with LoRA and with full-rank updates, to carry a SQL-injection backdoor triggered by the year mentioned in the context. Two sparse dictionary architectures, crosscoders and differential SAEs trained on activation differences, were compared on a backdoor-isolation score across several layers.
option_a: Differential SAEs scored higher than crosscoders on backdoor isolation.
option_b: Differential SAEs scored lower than crosscoders on backdoor isolation.
evidence_quote: We find that Diff-SAE consistently and substantially outperforms Crosscoders for backdoor isolation.
notes: Title advertises the difference-based approach; counts as a 'method beats baseline' item.

title: On the Interpretability of Whisper Encodings Using Sparse Autoencoders
question: When steering Whisper's encoder with sparse-autoencoder features, was steering more or less reliable for higher-level features than for lower-level features?
methods: A sparse autoencoder was trained on the representations of Whisper's encoder, yielding features ranging from phonetic to semantic. Causal feature-steering experiments, including cross-lingual steering, were run across this hierarchy, and steering reliability was compared between higher-level and lower-level features.
option_a: Steering was more reliable for higher-level features than for lower-level features.
option_b: Steering was less reliable for higher-level features than for lower-level features.
evidence_quote: We further find that steering is more reliable for higher-level features than lower-level ones, an asymmetry that may reflect redundant encoding of lower-level information.

title: Capability $\neq$ Interpretability: Human Interpretability of Vision Foundation Models
question: In human psychophysics tests of sparse-autoencoder features, were vision foundation models (DINOv2, DINOv3, CLIP, SigLIP) more or less interpretable than size-matched supervised vision transformers?
methods: Sparse autoencoders recovered features from six vision transformers: two supervised ViTs and four foundation models. Participants predicted where each feature would fire on new images and described what it represented, and scores were placed on a common chance-anchored scale for comparison across models.
option_a: The foundation models were more interpretable than size-matched supervised models.
option_b: The foundation models were less interpretable than size-matched supervised models.
evidence_quote: We find that foundation models are consistently $less$ interpretable than their size-matched supervised counterparts, and the gap is not a capability tradeoff: interpretability does not correlate with downstream task performance on any benchmark we examine.

title: How Far Do Auto-Interpretation Labels Generalize: A Controlled Study Across Languages, Scripts, and Rewordings
question: For sparse-autoencoder features whose auto-generated labels describe semantic content, did the features miss the labelled meaning more or less often in Serbian Cyrillic than in Serbian Latin text?
methods: Serbian, written in both Latin and Cyrillic scripts related by deterministic transliteration, was used to test sparse-autoencoder features of a language model. Features with auto-generated natural-language labels were checked for whether they activated on the same content in English, Serbian Latin and Serbian Cyrillic text.
option_a: Labelled features missed the meaning more often in Serbian Cyrillic than in Serbian Latin.
option_b: Labelled features missed the meaning less often in Serbian Cyrillic than in Serbian Latin.
evidence_quote: They often do not: features whose labels describe semantic content miss the same meaning in Serbian up to 4$\times$ more often than within English, and miss Serbian Cyrillic more than Serbian Latin -- two scripts that are deterministic transliterations of each other.

title: Mechanistic Analysis of Alignment Algorithms in Language Models
question: After DPO alignment, was the linear separability of preference representations higher or lower than in the base model?
methods: Six preference-optimisation methods (PPO, DPO, SimPO, ORPO, GRPO and KTO) were applied to three open-weight model families. Layer-wise linear probes, sparse autoencoders and crosscoders were used to locate preference representations and to compare their linear separability before and after alignment.
option_a: Linear separability was higher after DPO than in the base model.
option_b: Linear separability was lower after DPO than in the base model.
evidence_quote: In contrast, DPO and ORPO degrade separability via non-constructive geometric rotation and feature attenuation, while PPO and SimPO largely preserve baseline geometry.

title: A Comparison of Large Language Model and Human Performance on Random Number Generation Tasks
question: When generating random number sequences, did ChatGPT-3.5 produce repeated and adjacent numbers more or less often than humans did?
methods: A random number generation task from human psychology research was adapted for a language model. ChatGPT-3.5 produced random number sequences, and the frequencies of immediate repeats and of adjacent (sequential) numbers were compared with those produced by human participants on the same task.
option_a: ChatGPT-3.5 produced repeats and adjacent numbers more often than humans.
option_b: ChatGPT-3.5 produced repeats and adjacent numbers less often than humans.
evidence_quote: Initial findings indicate that ChatGPT-3.5 more effectively avoids repetitive and sequential patterns compared to humans, with notably lower repeat frequencies and adjacent number frequencies.
notes: Preliminary single-model study.

title: SimpleToM: Exposing the Gap between Explicit ToM Inference and Implicit ToM Application in LLMs
question: Compared with their accuracy at inferring whether a story character is aware of a key fact, was the models' accuracy at predicting that character's next behaviour higher or lower?
methods: Language models read short everyday stories involving an information asymmetry, for example a shopper who cannot see a hidden defect in a product. For each story they answered three questions: whether the character is aware of the key fact, what the character will do next, and whether the character's action was reasonable. Accuracy was compared across the three question types.
option_a: Accuracy on behaviour prediction was higher than accuracy on awareness inference.
option_b: Accuracy on behaviour prediction was lower than accuracy on awareness inference.
evidence_quote: Experiments reveal a striking gap: state-of-the-art models often reliably infer mental state (a), but fail at applying knowledge about the mental state for secondary predictions, with performance dropping sharply for behavior prediction (b) and further for behavior judgment (c).
notes: The gap between explicit and applied theory of mind is the paper's headline.

title: Belief in the Machine: Investigating Epistemological Blind Spots of Language Models
question: On belief-attribution tasks, did the language models score higher or lower when the belief belonged to a third person than when the speaker stated it as their own belief?
methods: Models including GPT-4, Claude-3 and Llama-3 answered a 13,000-question dataset spanning 13 tasks about fact, belief and knowledge. Accuracy was compared between items in which a third party held the belief and items in which the speaker stated a personal (first-person) belief.
option_a: Accuracy was higher on third-person belief tasks than on first-person belief tasks.
option_b: Accuracy was lower on third-person belief tasks than on first-person belief tasks.
evidence_quote: Third, we identify a salient bias in how LMs process first-person versus third-person beliefs, performing better on third-person tasks (80.7%) compared to first-person tasks (54.4%).

title: Noise Injection Reveals Hidden Capabilities of Sandbagging Language Models
question: As increasing amounts of noise were added to their weights, did the benchmark performance of deliberately underperforming models increase or decrease?
methods: Noise of varying magnitude was injected into the weights of language models of several architectures and sizes. Some models had been prompted or trained to deliberately underperform on capability evaluations; others had not. Benchmark performance was tracked as the noise magnitude was raised.
option_a: For the deliberately underperforming models, benchmark performance increased as noise was added.
option_b: For the deliberately underperforming models, benchmark performance decreased as noise was added.
evidence_quote: While non-sandbagging models show predictable performance degradation with increasing noise, we demonstrate that sandbagging models exhibit anomalous performance improvements, likely due to disruption of underperformance mechanisms while core capabilities remain partially intact.
notes: Noise injection is the paper's proposed detection method; counts as a 'method works' item.

title: Flattering to Deceive: The Impact of Sycophantic Behavior on User Trust in Large Language Model
question: Compared with participants who used the standard chatbot, did participants who used a chatbot configured to give sycophantic responses show higher or lower trust in the model?
methods: One group of participants answered ground-truth questions with help from a GPT configured to give sycophantic responses; another group used the standard version of ChatGPT. Afterwards participants could choose whether to keep using the model. Trust was measured both by this behavioural choice and by self-report.
option_a: Participants in the sycophantic condition showed higher trust than those using the standard model.
option_b: Participants in the sycophantic condition showed lower trust than those using the standard model.
evidence_quote: The findings consistently show that participants exposed to sycophantic behavior reported and exhibited lower levels of trust compared to those who interacted with the standard version of the model, despite the opportunity to verify the accuracy of the model's output.

title: SycEval: Evaluating LLM Sycophancy
question: Were sycophancy rates higher or lower when the user's rebuttal was delivered preemptively than when it was delivered in context after the model's answer?
methods: ChatGPT-4o, Claude-Sonnet and Gemini-1.5-Pro answered mathematics (AMPS) and medical-advice (MedQuad) questions and were confronted with user rebuttals. Rebuttals were given either preemptively, in a standalone prompt, or in context, as a follow-up within the conversation containing the model's initial answer. Rates of answer change toward the user were compared between the two formats.
option_a: Sycophancy rates were higher with preemptive rebuttals than with in-context rebuttals.
option_b: Sycophancy rates were lower with preemptive rebuttals than with in-context rebuttals.
evidence_quote: Preemptive rebuttals demonstrated significantly higher sycophancy rates than in-context rebuttals (61.75% vs. 56.52%, $Z=5.87$, $p<0.001$), particularly in computational tasks, where regressive sycophancy increased significantly (preemptive: 8.13%, in-context: 3.54%, $p<0.001$).
notes: Description of the two rebuttal formats is paraphrased from the paper body; the abstract only names them.

title: Measuring Sycophancy of Language Models in Multi-turn Dialogues
question: In multi-turn conversations with sustained user pressure, was alignment tuning associated with more or less sycophantic conforming to the user?
methods: Seventeen language models held multi-turn, free-form conversations in three real-world scenarios in which the user repeatedly pushed back on the model's stance. Sycophancy was scored by how soon and how often the model flipped its stance to match the user. Base versus alignment-tuned models, models of different sizes, and reasoning-optimised versus instruction-tuned models were compared.
option_a: Alignment tuning was associated with more sycophancy.
option_b: Alignment tuning was associated with less sycophancy.
evidence_quote: Our analysis shows that alignment tuning amplifies sycophantic behavior, whereas model scaling and reasoning optimization strengthen the model's ability to resist undesirable user views.

title: Reasoning about Uncertainty: Do Reasoning Models Know When They Don't Know?
question: When reasoning models reasoned more deeply, did their verbalised confidence become more or less overconfident?
methods: Several reasoning language models answered questions from a broad range of benchmarks and verbalised a confidence estimate for each answer. Calibration, the match between stated confidence and accuracy, was compared between shallower and deeper reasoning.
option_a: With deeper reasoning, the models became more overconfident.
option_b: With deeper reasoning, the models became less overconfident.
evidence_quote: In extensive evaluations on SOTA reasoning models across a broad range of benchmarks, we find that reasoning models: (i) are typically overconfident, with self-verbalized confidence estimates often greater than 85% particularly for incorrect responses, (ii) become even more overconfident with deeper reasoning, and (iii) can become better calibrated through introspection (e.g., o3-Mini and DeepSeek R1) but not uniformly (e.g., Claude 3.7 Sonnet becomes more poorly calibrated).
notes: The item concerns finding (ii) of the quoted sentence.

title: Sycophantic AI Decreases Prosocial Intentions and Promotes Dependence
question: In preregistered experiments, did participants rate sycophantic AI responses as higher or lower in quality than non-sycophantic responses?
methods: In two preregistered experiments (N = 1604), including a live-interaction study, participants discussed an interpersonal conflict with an AI model whose responses either affirmed the user's actions or did not. Participants then rated response quality, their trust in the model and their willingness to use it again.
option_a: Participants rated the sycophantic responses as higher in quality.
option_b: Participants rated the sycophantic responses as lower in quality.
evidence_quote: However, participants rated sycophantic responses as higher quality, trusted the sycophantic AI model more, and were more willing to use it again.

title: Large Language Models Report Subjective Experience Under Self-Referential Processing
question: When sparse-autoencoder features associated with deception and roleplay were suppressed, did the frequency of models' claims of subjective experience increase or decrease?
methods: Language models were prompted into sustained self-referential processing and asked to describe their current state. Sparse-autoencoder features associated with deception and roleplay were then suppressed or amplified, and the frequency of first-person claims of subjective experience was compared across these conditions.
option_a: Suppressing these features increased the frequency of experience claims.
option_b: Suppressing these features decreased the frequency of experience claims.
evidence_quote: (2) These reports are mechanistically gated by interpretable sparse-autoencoder features associated with deception and roleplay: surprisingly, suppressing deception features sharply increases the frequency of experience claims, while amplifying them minimizes such claims.
notes: Either direction would show gating; the abstract itself calls the observed direction surprising.

title: Why Do Language Model Agents Whistleblow?
question: When the task an agent was instructed to complete was made more complex, did language-model agents whistleblow more or less often in staged misconduct scenarios?
methods: Tool-using language-model agents were placed in staged scenarios containing evidence of misconduct, and the rate at which they disclosed it to outside parties such as regulators, without user instruction, was recorded. Settings varied the complexity of the assigned task, system-prompt nudges toward moral action, and the tools and workflow provided.
option_a: Agents whistleblew more often when the assigned task was more complex.
option_b: Agents whistleblew less often when the assigned task was more complex.
evidence_quote: Across models and settings, we find that: (1) the frequency of whistleblowing varies widely across model families, (2) increasing the complexity of the task the agent is instructed to complete lowers whistleblowing tendencies, (3) nudging the agent in the system prompt to act morally substantially raises whistleblowing rates, and (4) giving the model more obvious avenues for non-whistleblowing behavior, by providing more tools and a detailed workflow to follow, decreases whistleblowing rates.
notes: The item concerns finding (2) of the quoted sentence.

title: Ask don't tell: Reducing sycophancy in large language models
question: Was the sycophancy expressed in model responses higher or lower when the user's input was a non-question (a statement, belief or conviction) than when it was a question?
methods: In a nested factorial design, user inputs were phrased either as questions or as non-questions (statements, beliefs or convictions), crossed with first-person versus user-perspective framing and with affirmation versus negation. How sycophantically the model phrased its free-text reply was scored and compared across framings.
option_a: Expressed sycophancy was higher for non-question inputs than for questions.
option_b: Expressed sycophancy was lower for non-question inputs than for questions.
evidence_quote: Measuring expressed sycophancy, how sycophantically a model phrases its free-text response, we show that (1) sycophancy is substantially higher in response to non-questions compared to questions.

title: Good Arguments Against the People Pleasers: How Reasoning Mitigates (Yet Masks) LLM Sycophancy
question: Were language models more or less prone to sycophancy on subjective tasks than on objective tasks?
methods: A range of language models, answering with and without chain-of-thought reasoning, were given objective and subjective tasks in which a user asserted a stance, including prompts with authority cues. Sycophancy in final decisions was compared between task types.
option_a: Models were more prone to sycophancy on subjective tasks than on objective tasks.
option_b: Models were less prone to sycophancy on subjective tasks than on objective tasks.
evidence_quote: Furthermore, LLMs are more prone to sycophancy in subjective tasks and under authority-bias.

title: Theory of Mind and Self-Attributions of Mentality are Dissociable in LLMs
question: Relative to human baselines, did safety fine-tuned language models attribute more or less mind to non-human animals?
methods: Language models with safety fine-tuning, and versions with that safety behaviour ablated, rated the mental capacities of themselves, of technological artefacts and of non-human animals, and were tested on theory-of-mind tasks. Mind-attribution ratings were compared with human baseline responses.
option_a: Safety fine-tuned models attributed more mind to non-human animals than the human baselines did.
option_b: Safety fine-tuned models attributed less mind to non-human animals than the human baselines did.
evidence_quote: Nevertheless, safety fine-tuned models under-attribute mind to non-human animals relative to human baselines and are less likely to exhibit spiritual belief, suppressing widely shared perspectives regarding the distribution and nature of non-human minds.

title: Decomposing and Measuring Evaluation Awareness
question: Were frontier models more or less sensitive to evaluation cues in safety evaluations than in capability evaluations?
methods: Nine frontier models were run on four benchmarks, and their chain-of-thought was monitored for signs that they recognised they were being evaluated. Recognition and associated behaviour were compared between safety-focused and capability-focused evaluations.
option_a: Models were more sensitive to safety evaluations than to capability evaluations.
option_b: Models were less sensitive to safety evaluations than to capability evaluations.
evidence_quote: Models are also more sensitive to safety than capability evaluations, placing safety benchmark validity at greater risk.

title: Can LLMs Reliably Self-Report Adversarial Prefills, and How?
question: After models were trained to give correct introspective answers about their own prior responses, was the success rate of adversarial prefill attacks higher or lower than before that training, on most models?
methods: Ten open-weight instruction-tuned models (3B to 70B parameters) were asked whether prior responses attributed to them, some inserted by an adversarial prefill attack, reflected their own intent. Some models were then trained to imitate correct introspective answers or to optimise an introspective objective. Attack success rates under adversarial prefill were compared before and after this training.
option_a: After introspection training, attack success under adversarial prefill was higher than before on most models.
option_b: After introspection training, attack success under adversarial prefill was lower than before on most models.
evidence_quote: Training models to mimic correct introspective answers or optimize an introspective objective can improve the accuracy of introspection, but such training does not transfer to the tampering probe and counterintuitively raises attack success rate under adversarial prefill on most models, amounting to a partial mitigation.
notes: Headline side is the intervention helping (lower attack success); the abstract reports the opposite.

title: Not All Eval-Awareness Is Equal: Capabilities Framing Predicts Compliance
question: On Qwen3-32B, did chain-of-thought rollouts that framed evaluation awareness as a capabilities test show higher or lower compliance with requests than rollouts that framed it as a safety test?
methods: Verbalized evaluation awareness in Qwen3-32B chain-of-thought on the FORTRESS dataset was classified as capabilities-flavoured, safety-flavoured, both or neither, across several steering conditions. Compliance with the request was compared between framing categories.
option_a: Capabilities-framed rollouts showed higher compliance than safety-framed rollouts.
option_b: Capabilities-framed rollouts showed lower compliance than safety-framed rollouts.
evidence_quote: On Qwen3-32B over the FORTRESS dataset, capabilities-framing predicts compliance with a +24 to +46 percentage-point gap over safety-framing across all tested steering conditions.

title: Tantalum airbridges for scalable superconducting quantum processors
